title: TreeSize won't renew perpetual-license support unless users subscribe
summary: "Current economic conditions" have shifted TreeSize's business model.
full_text:
The company behind the disk space analyzer TreeSize has irked some users by no longer offering support or updates for perpetual licenses beyond their maintenance period unless customers subscribe. Further frustration has come from JAM Software’s long-standing policy of not providing license keys or installers to TreeSize perpetual license holders after that support period ends.
Since 2025, JAM Software has been transitioning most TreeSize editions to subscription models. Today, it sells perpetual licenses only for personal use, which include 12 months of updates, support, and “downloads of older versions, and your license,” plus the option to extend the support period. TreeSize currently has “no plans to discontinue the sale of perpetual licenses for TreeSize Personal,” product manager Hendrik Christ told Ars Technica.
As perpetual-license maintenance periods expire, customers are discovering that extending support now generally requires subscribing to software they already own the right to use.
On Reddit, a user shared an email informing them that support for their perpetual license ends in September, after which they will lose access to updates and support because those “are only available in the subscription.”
Christ told Ars that considering the “current economic conditions,” the change was “necessary to keep developing and supporting TreeSize reliably over the long term.”
One of the biggest criticisms is that JAM Software will not provide backup installation files or license keys to customers with unsupported licenses. TreeSize’s email urged the user to make backups.
“Honestly, it feels quite low to strip paying customers of the ability to simply download the installer for a software version they already paid for,” the Reddit user said.
But even before it sold TreeSize subscriptions, JAM Software didn’t permanently retain every installation file and key after a customer’s support period ended, Christ said. This is because “older software versions can contain known bugs or even security vulnerabilities,” he said, adding:

title: When your vehicle outlives its cloud: What happens next?
summary: Automakers love connected vehicles, but support isn't open-ended.
full_text:
Do you use your vehicle’s app to pre‑cool the cabin on a scorching day, confirm the doors are locked from bed, or have the car automatically call for help when the airbags go off?
Savor those connected, cloud‑based conveniences while you can—the clock is already ticking on their obsolescence. In a few short years, you may be driving today’s vehicle without many of the features you currently enjoy.
How we got hooked on the cloud
“Connected services”—cloud-based and networked features that let a vehicle communicate with external systems to deliver apps, data, and remote functions to drivers and passengers—have been around since the 1990s, when GM introduced OnStar as an option. Those early systems were mostly voice‑centric, but they still depended on centralized back‑end systems. Modern versions, which are fully data-driven and cloud-hosted, use much more sophisticated over-the-air data links to allow a considerably better feature set.
Today, virtually every volume brand offers some form of cloud-based telematics or a connected services stack. They can be deeply embedded, and most are fully integrated as the core of modern vehicle connectivity, supporting over-the-air (OTA) updates for the vehicle and app-based services for owners. As GM’s OnStar celebrates more than 30 years of service, a dozen others have joined, with each automaker branding its own unique services. HondaLink, Lexus Enform, FordPass, BMW ConnectedDrive, Volvo On Call, and Porsche Connect are just a few.
Despite their catchy marketing names, the systems are all functionally similar—each offers a very comparable feature set. Basics include remote lock/start, vehicle status and maintenance updates, location and tracking, and emergency assistance. Additional premium features include in-vehicle Wi-Fi hotspots, cabin preconditioning, stolen-vehicle tracking services, and concierge owner services.
Plenty of consumers have embraced the remote conveniences and demonstrated to automakers that they are more than willing to pay for them. After a bundled “free trial” following new vehicle delivery, manufacturers charge monthly fees or subscriptions for connected services. GM said that 40 percent of OnStar customers choose to renew their subscriptions after the introductory period expired.

title: Apps targeted at US troops contain Chinese and Russian code
summary: More than one-eighth of apps analyzed contained foreign code.
full_text:
A recent examination of hundreds of mobile apps marketed toward US military personnel found more than one in eight contained software built by companies in China, Russia, or other foreign nations, raising fresh concerns that adversary governments could harvest data revealing where service members live, work, and deploy.
According to researchers at Purdue University, the US Military Academy at West Point, and Florida International University, one popular app used by service members to rate living conditions on their own bases include code from Huawei, the Chinese telecom that US regulators flagged as a national security threat in 2020. Two others were built by Russian companies and incorporate the Russian ad service Yandex.
The largely unregulated advertising industry that tracks Americans online treats civilians and service members mostly the same—unless there is profit in telling them apart—despite evidence that exposure can reveal troop deployments, unit movements, and the routines of personnel within intelligence facilities and hardened shelters where nuclear weapons are believed to be stored.
WIRED investigations have previously shown location data harvested from ordinary apps tracing US service members to their homes, their children’s schools, and off-base establishments where troops are prohibited from being seen. Experts have warned the same data could aid foreign spies in identifying personnel with access to sensitive sites, map when a facility is least guarded, or surface other compromising details.
The stakes are no longer hypothetical. In April, US Central Command acknowledged in a letter to Senator Ron Wyden that it had received multiple threat reports of adversaries exploiting commercial location data to target or surveil American personnel in the Middle East, where US forces remain locked in a standoff with the Iranian military over the Strait of Hormuz. Lawmakers called it the first official confirmation that troops in an active war zone were being hunted through the data-broker economy—a threat the Pentagon’s own contractors and researchers had warned about for nearly a decade.

title: 2027 Kia Seltos first drive gives you plenty of SUV for not much $
summary: It starts at just under $25,000, but the hybrid won't arrive until next year.
full_text:
NEWPORT BEACH, Calif.—Although it sometimes feels like automakers have all but abandoned everything other than high-end luxury model vehicles, it’s not universally true. While some car companies have lobbied the government, terrified, asking to build protective walls to fend off cheap Chinese competition, others have looked at the problem from a different angle, trying to meet the moment. One such effort is the new Kia Seltos, a small SUV that takes inspiration from the Telluride but with a starting price of just $24,990 plus delivery charge.
The US almost didn’t get the Seltos in the first place; the first-generation model was designed with China in mind. Seltos take two is more considered, and also a little more substantial. The new body with its Telluride-like design cues has been stretched, mostly in the wheelbase. That said, at 174.4 inches (4,430 mm) long, 72 inches (1,829 mm) wide, and 64.9 inches (1,648 mm) tall, it’s still a subcompact, one segment smaller than something like a Toyota RAV4 or Mazda CX-5.
Kia is offering a choice of three different powertrain variants. The 1.6 L hybrid is the one we’re most interested in. But that version won’t be in showrooms until Q4 this year; don’t expect an Ars first drive of the hybrid Seltos until early next year. Or any other details in this first drive report—the hybrid Seltos is still undergoing its EPA certification, and Kia isn’t prepared to talk power, torque, or efficiency until that’s done and dusted.
Most will come with a 2.0 L four-cylinder under the hood that generates 147 hp (110 kW) and 132 lb-ft (180 Nm). You can have that engine with either front-wheel drive and a combined 30 mpg (7.8 L/100 km), or all-wheel drive and 28 mpg (8.4 L/100 km) combined. This engine is available in various trims, from the sub-$25,000 entry-level FWD Seltos LX to the $30,090 AWD Seltos EX.

title: A Sneaky Hacking Tool Targeting AI Infrastructure Is Lurking in Victims’ Blind Spots
summary: A new type of malware can worm deep into AI coding systems to steal data and logins—and can flip a “death switch” to destroy files and keep out real users.
full_text:
As AI tools proliferate and become deeply ingrained in software development around the world, new research from the cybersecurity firm Crowdstrike shows how attackers are actively targeting the AI toolchain to steal access credentials, gain deeper access to a target environment, exfiltrate sensitive data, and even destroy target files and systems—all while finding new ways to cover their tracks.
Researchers discovered a worm in the wild while investigating AI software supply chain attacks. Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's senior vice president of counter adversary work, says that the company has not yet attributed the activity to a specific actor, but that it fits into larger evolutions in how attackers like TeamPCP (which Crowdstrike tracks as “Altered Spider”) and North Korean groups are targeting the AI software supply chain.
“This is one of the campaigns that we’ve seen showing that this is an emerging attack class,” Meyers tells WIRED. “As AI coding agents become the development standard, supply chain threats are evolving to exploit those trust relationships. For the first time we’re experiencing how much AI and the AI toolchain has played into the broader tech ecosystem.”
The worm CrowdStrike identified works in phases. First it does reconnaissance to assess the target environment. Then it looks for access tokens and other sensitive data, like cryptographic keys and server access credentials that it can deliver to attackers. As the malware gains privileges, it further unpacks itself and continues to grab credentials, particularly “npm" tokens that give access to key software package management servers and other development capabilities like pull requests.
The deeper the malware bores into the system, the more sensitive data it can grab. At this point, the malware can also deploy its destructive capability, or what Meyers calls a “death switch,” to destroy files or block legitimate access to the compromised infrastructure.
The key finding, though, is that much of the worm's malicious activity takes place in what are essentially blind spots, because so much of its behavior mimics legitimate actions. “It's like a needle in a haystack, except this is a needle in a needle stack,” Meyers says. “This looks very much like a lot of the automation organizations are using to build code, so it’s very difficult to detect.”
Meyers adds, too, that in these AI software development pipelines, it is harder to gather the data points that security scanners and analysis tools traditionally use to detect potentially suspicious activity.
“There’s a lot of telemetry overlap because legitimate AI coding systems are operating the same way as this worm, so it becomes very difficult to discern from the telemetry you have available to you what is legitimate and what is illegitimate,” Meyers says.
To hide in plain sight even more insidiously, the authors of the worm included time delays where various capabilities will execute hours or even days after the groundwork is laid, making it even harder for defenders to establish a cause and effect of certain events leading to certain outcomes.
Meyers says that Crowdstrike has been working on strategies to connect more of the dots, but he emphasizes that as AI software development explodes, there is a pressing need for all players to collaborate on structural solutions.
“It’s a limited detection surface because only so much of this activity is actually going to produce any sort of telemetry signal for us to look at,” Meyers says, “so it becomes extremely onerous to determine what is legitimate and what is illegitimate behavior.”

title: The Light Flip Is the Stylish Dumb Flip Phone of Your Dreams
summary: A flip phone with 5G, USB-C, a headphone jack, and a removable battery? Say it ain’t so.
full_text:
It turns out that the Light Phone III—the dumbphone with pretty hardware, like an all-metal build and a monochrome OLED touchscreen—is “too similar to a smartphone.”
That's one of the pieces of feedback that Brooklyn-based Light Phone has received in the past year since it launched the device, even if it doesn't have access to anywhere near the number of apps your smartphone does. It's why the company is now introducing the Light Flip—a dumb flip phone with no front screen that looks like a sleeker version of Motorola or Ericsson handsets from the late '90s and early aughts.
“They don't want to be seen as using a smartphone,” says Kaiwei Tang, CEO and cofounder of Light Phone, talking about the more than two dozen Gen Z consumers the company interviewed. But the dumb flip phones currently on the market—made by manufacturers like HMD or TCL—don't meet the bar. Tang says that many of the users he's spoken with have had to replace their devices quite often because they break easily. Some who opt for older devices say that those devices aren't certified to work on the major cell networks.
“They describe their flip phone as ugly, stupid, no one is updating the software, some still have social media, no one is repairing the phone," says Tang. “But they stick with it.” His cofounder, Joe Hollier, says these consumers know it's frivolous, but they're “just so anti–Big Tech.”
The Light Flip is also designed to be more accessible to the masses. Light Phone says RAM shortages are forcing it to raise the price of the Light Phone III from $699 to $899. (The device already saw price increases last year due to tariffs.) The Light Flip, on the other hand, costs $299. It ships in April of 2027, and you can reserve a unit now.
The company is introducing a 24-month contract option that lets you buy the Flip for $39 per month, which includes a service plan powered by AT&T and T-Mobile's network with 1 GB of data and unlimited calls and texts. (Yes, that means Light Phone is also a mobile virtual network operator in the US, Canada, and the UK.) There's also a plan for the Light Phone III at $59 per month for anyone who can't stomach the near-$1,000 price.
“I think people are just so accustomed to the subscription model when it comes to cell phones that we at least have to offer it,” Hollier says.
The Light Flip doesn't have a touchscreen; instead, users have to rely on a D-pad, three function keys, a confirm and cancel button, and old-school T9 typing with predictive text. All the “tools” from the Light Phone III—what Light Phone calls its apps on its LightOS platform—will work when the Light Flip launches next year.
It's a pretty limited set, with tools like Phone, Alarm, Calculator, Calendar, and Directions. However, in May, the company announced a software development kit that enables third-party developers to create new tools for the platform, expanding the possibilities. These may need tweaks to perform just as well on the Light Flip.
There's USB-C, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, 5G connectivity, Nano SIM and eSIM support, even a headphone jack, a perk missing on the pricier Light Phone III. (There is no NFC.) On the front, the lack of a screen keeps up with the distraction-free ethos—it's just a notification LED that flashes when new alerts come through. There's a 12-MP camera on the back, and a replaceable 1,800-mAh battery. Flip it open and there's a 2.8-inch OLED display, stereo speakers, and two microphones.
The whole device is plastic, unlike its all-metal sibling, which helps keep the cost down. That also allows the company to offer it in six colors: black, navy, red, pink, yellow, and light gray. It's IP54 water- and dust-resistant.
Tang points to the recent Summer of Ludd festival that took place in New York City, where he and other Light Phone members were present as participants. Event-goers booed people who pulled out their smartphones to record video.
“The sentiment of pushing back on smartphones is so strong; they don't like AI,” he says. “They want these different form factors that make them feel proud or completely separated from smartphone app stores. It makes us feel encouraged that this is exactly what we've wanted to do for 10 years, and now it's getting bigger and bigger and younger and younger.” It's no accident that Light Phone's new flippy handset is being announced a day before Samsung's Galaxy Unpacked event, where the mobile giant is expected to debut its latest folding smartphones.
Just a month ago, retro gaming brand Commodore announced the Callback 8020, its own version of a smart flip phone resembling an old-school Nokia. The company is channeling the same digital well-being mentality as Light Phone, except Commodore's device runs an operating system that can still download modern-day Android apps. The catch is that social media apps and browsers are blocked; strictly utilitarian apps are available, like Spotify, Uber, and Google Maps. It costs $399 and will ship later this year.
Tang and Hollier were happy to see Commodore's new handset. “They took a different approach to us by doubling down on the retro side, and I think that's awesome,” Hollier says. “We've always said we want more options for people, and the more normalized non-smartphones become, the easier it will be for everyone to make a transition.”

title: Nvidia Wants to Own Every Chip Inside AI Data Centers
summary: Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform combines CPUs and GPUs into a single system, reflecting the company’s growing ambition to power every layer of AI infrastructure.
full_text:
Nvidia is hyping up its new Vera Rubin chip system this week, revealing new performance benchmarks for the GPU and CPU combo ahead of rival AMD’s annual product event in San Francisco on Thursday.
During a lengthy technical workshop last week at the company’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California, Nvidia executives boasted to a small group of journalists about the chip system’s increased power and efficiency capabilities. The biggest takeaway: Nvidia, which has long specialized in making GPUs, is increasingly trying to position itself as a supplier of CPUs that can power AI agents.
While GPUs are still the main hardware that companies use to train and run their AI models, the industry's shift toward more complex, agentic systems has increased demand for CPUs, which can orchestrate data flows, networking, and other software tasks. That's likely one reason Nvidia has been eager to promote itself as a supplier of complete AI systems rather than just AI chips.
Vera Rubin is Nvidia’s successor to its hybrid superchip system Grace Blackwell and represents the linchpin of its near-term future powering the AI industry. It’s designed to offer one CPU for every two GPUs. In a single Vera Rubin NVL 72 super chip system, there are 36 Vera CPUs for every 72 Rubin GPUs. Nvidia is also selling the Vera CPU as a stand-alone product, and it has reportedly told Chinese customers these could be ready as soon as August.
Nvidia executives emphasized that its new Vera Rubin NVL72 racks—a stack of chips packed into a single liquid-cooled platform—are much more “plug-and-play” than some of its earlier products. During a brief tour of a Nvidia data center lab in Silicon Valley, Nvidia executives shared that OpenAI already has one Vera Rubin rack in use.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang didn’t make an appearance at the workshop in Santa Clara last week; he was in Japan announcing the chipmaker’s new partnerships with a number of Japanese firms to develop AI for robotics. The briefings were instead led by Ian Buck, Nvidia’s longtime vice president of accelerated computing and the architect behind the company’s CUDA software.
“We’re on a road map to crank out new architectures, not just GPUs but CPUs,” Buck told reporters. “We’re going to keep innovating, because it’s do this or die in Silicon Valley.”
The meetings were held in Huang’s executive briefing center, where multiple desks nearby were piled with bags of Taiwanese snacks that the CEO brought back from his recent trip to Computex, a massive annual semiconductor trade show in Taipei, an Nvidia spokesperson told WIRED.
Nvidia claims that the Vera Rubin NVL72 system will process 10 times as many tokens per watt as the company’s Grace Blackwell super chip. The company says that its Vera CPU is faster at processing agentic AI tasks compared to rival CPUs from AMD and Intel (though the tests it ran to support those benchmarks appears to have used slightly older generations of its competitors’ CPUs). Localized memory subsystems on the new chips will also offer nearly three times as much memory bandwidth as Blackwell, which will likely be an appealing feature to many companies amid an ongoing shortage of high-bandwidth memory.
Nvidia says it has also significantly reduced the number of cables needed to connect its chips to racks in multi-rack server systems, to the point where the company is touting Vera Rubin as “cable-free compute” and “hot-swappable.” This means customers can theoretically reduce the amount of time it takes to install each rack from a couple of hours to a few minutes, a point that was brought up by both Buck and Andrew Bell, Nvidia’s senior vice president of hardware engineering. And the new chip system is 100 percent liquid-cooled, which can reduce the amount of energy needed to cool the chips, since air-cooling is more energy intensive.
Ever since Nvidia unveiled Vera Rubin in the spring of 2025, the company has been slowly dribbling out more details about the chip system while insisting it will be released on schedule. Huang has repeatedly said Vera Rubin is ramping to “full production” and will ship in the second half of this year, with early customers including Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle.
Nvidia is particularly sensitive to any suggestion of delays after its previous-generation Blackwell chips reportedly overheated when connected together in the company's customized server racks, forcing it to make design changes and push back shipments.
Nvidia’s marketing push for Vera Rubin is happening just ahead of rival AMD’s annual conference, where executives are expected to tout its next-generation AI and data center chips. On Sunday, AMD revealed more details about its Helios AI chip rack, which is designed to compete with Nvidia’s new wares. Both AMD and Nvidia have been vying for large-scale, multiyear contracts to supply chips to AI hyperscalers like Meta and Amazon and AI labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceXAI.
Over the past two years, AMD has significantly grown its share of the market for CPUs used in data centers. The company has long been recognized as a pioneer of the modern chiplet architecture used in x86 processors, which still account for the vast majority of data center CPU revenue. Nvidia, by contrast, builds its data center CPUs on ARM, an alternative chip architecture known for its power efficiency.
Nvidia executives Buck and Hannah Coutand, who runs Nvidia's CPU product marketing, both emphasized that Vera Rubin abandons the chiplet architecture used by many modern processors in favor of a single, monolithic chip. Coutand argued that stitching together multiple chiplets imposes “a heavy tax on memory bandwidth and data movement,” whereas the monolithic design of Vera Rubin allows data to move more quickly across a single integrated circuit.

title: The Great Peptide Cash Grab Has Begun
summary: The FDA could decide whether to loosen rules around peptide production this week. Some telehealth players are already seeing dollar signs.
full_text:
Has anyone tried to sell you peptides yet? If not, they probably will soon. Once a niche interest among bodybuilders and biohackers, peptides are an increasingly popular class of substance hyped by both fringe influencers and the current US secretary of Health and Human Services.
Earlier this year, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told the podcaster Joe Rogan that the government intended to loosen restrictions on peptide production. This week, it could finally happen: On July 23 and 24, the Food and Drug Administration will discuss whether to reclassify a group of peptides so that pharmacies can legally make custom mixes, a process known as compounding. The move would reverse a decision made in 2023 by the Biden administration, which barred certain peptides from being compounded.
Although career scientists at the agency have recommended against it, many industry insiders tell WIRED they believe the FDA will approve reclassification anyway, since the committee put together to do the assessment includes peptide boosters. Some players in the telehealth world are already operating under the assumption that the floodgates will soon open. “We’re getting everything ready to go,” says Myra Ahmad, the chief executive of the telehealth platform Mochi Health, which originally focused on GLP-1 medications. “We have pharmacies that have done all their safety testing stuff; they’re putting pricing together.”
Some of the largest telehealth companies have looked forward to this moment for over a year. Virtual health care juggernaut Hims & Hers Health purchased a peptide manufacturing facility in February 2025 and is developing clinical protocols for peptides, according to its chief medical officer, Anant Vinjamoori, who is slated to testify at the FDA hearing. Joshua Fritzler, president of the compounding pharmacy Olympia Pharmaceuticals, says the company has been preparing in advance of the anticipated changes, “spending a lot of money to create these formulas” to be ready if the FDA gives the green light.
“There’s an understanding in the industry that something big is happening,” he says.
The GLP-1 boom warmed people up to the idea of injecting medications at home and proved to be a cash cow for pharmacies and virtual clinics. Now, though, many of these companies are eager to expand their horizons. Cole Thomas, the director of sales and operations at the pharmacy marketing and technology platform RxConnexion, says that some of the company’s compounding pharmacy clients are testing peptides that are likely to be popular. One such variety, BPC-157, is touted as a healing compound and is one-half of the combination known as the “Wolverine stack.” (BPC stands for “body protection compound.”)
Cameron Bravo, a research scientist at the biotech firm Sapho Bio, says his company has been approached about testing a variety of peptides already, too. (Mochi Health is a client.) Sapho Bio runs tests to “validate” formulas that clients bring, ensuring the mixtures are uncontaminated and properly sealed. So far, it has tested BPC-157 as well as more obscure offerings like MOTS-c, which is hyped as “exercise in a vial” by evangelists. Some of the pharmacies the company works with are testing multiple products, at significant cost. “They're probably investing something like $100,000 into these before they're even fully out yet,” he says.
Even if this week’s meeting goes exactly how peptide boosters want it to go, with the committee approving all of the substances up for discussion, that won’t lead to an immediate green light for sellers. The next step involves a review period, during which the FDA will propose rules and the public will be able to comment. “It’s a long-winded process,” says Gerard Olson, who was recently the director of research at LegitScript, a company that provides certifications for telehealth providers and pharmacies.
Hims plans to wait and see. “We don't want to be necessarily first to market. We want to be best in market,” says Vinjamoori, the chief medical officer.
But other compounders and clinics are moving ahead with prescribing these medications as injectables.
Amanecia Health, a concierge service that sees patients in person at its Texas and Virginia clinics in addition to operating a telehealth practice, has started prescribing popular options like BPC-157. “There's been an uptick in interest because it's been all over Instagram and the media,” says Amanceia’s founder Ann Czarnik, who also works as an emergency medicine physician. Even though Czarnik readily acknowledges that these substances do not have the same kind of safety and efficacy data that traditional medications do, her practice has begun tentatively prescribing them to a small group of patients; she stresses that this “tiny percentage” of her patient base is aware that they are not FDA-approved medications. “I can’t advertise that I’m prescribing them yet,” she says.
Scott Brunner, the head of the Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding, has been warning member pharmacies to comply with the law and not go rogue and roll out peptides early. “Many of them are being hammered by prescribers and patients to do this,” he says. To make the temptation even more intense, these compounders know that the people they turn away have easy access to a gray-market supply.
Right now, all of the peptides up for discussion in the July FDA meeting, as well as many others, are remarkably easy to get your hands on. They’re available for purchase from online sellers that place disclaimers on their products, noting that they are “research-grade only” and not for human consumption.
“We are not selling. It is not legal for us to do so,” says Olympia’s Fritzler. “This gray market, which is insane—obviously we are not participating in it.”
“Everyone and their mom wants to start a peptide company right now,” says Thomas Millman, who runs OnTop Labs, a Florida-based research-use peptide operation. OnTop Labs sells products like Melanotan II, known as the “Barbie peptide” and the “tan jab” for the way it stimulates melatonin production and changes skin pigmentation. It’s also slated for an FDA discussion on reclassification, but not until 2027. The Skin Cancer Foundation recently issued a warning about Melanotan II, citing case reports about increased melanoma risk.
Nevertheless, Millman promotes his products on social media, primarily TikTok. The glut of companies offering research-grade peptides has made it more difficult to stand out, he says. “There’s just so much more competition.”

title: Halliday’s New Smart Glasses Skip the Camera
summary: Halliday’s G2 glasses can listen to and summarize your workplace meetings—with no video involved.
full_text:
There’s a new pair of camera-less smart glasses in town: the Halliday G2, designed to listen to workplace meetings, absorb what happens, and summarize all the interesting bits, much like always-listening wearables. Halliday says the mics can be turned on for meetings, using AI voice commands, or making phone calls, but switch off when not in use.
They’re normal-ish looking glasses, meant to blend into a professional environment, namely by not having cameras on them. They cost $599, with first shipments planned for September 2026. There are paid subscription tiers for the AI services that range from $10 per month to $99, but users can choose a free tier that offers 120 minutes of recording time.
Halliday’s glasses might not be met well by one of its competitors. Smart glasses brand Even Realities launched its G2 glasses late last year, proudly focusing on the lack of cameras in its eyewear; Halliday’s G2 shares the same name and channels the same mantra, not to mention a striking resemblance. (In both cases, G2 is short for Generation 2, so it's indicating the stage of the device, not necessarily a specific brand name.)
Building smart glasses without cameras seems to be growing more popular. The market is still dominated by Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, even though those have garnered the “pervert glasses” moniker because the device’s built-in cameras have been abused to capture pictures and video of people (mostly women) without them realizing it. Eager to differentiate, some companies have shipped ways to cover up their cameras, or, like Even Realities and now Halliday, are skipping them entirely. Still, those glasses are all-in on recording the audio around you.
In its press release, Halliday says that unlike smart glasses with cameras in them, the G2 is meant to be “a professional tool for real-world work and social environments. With no camera, the glasses are better suited for meetings, client conversations, secure workplaces, and other spaces where recording devices may be unwelcome.”
That acknowledgement aside, Halliday’s G2 glasses do not have an indicator light or other method to inform people around the wearer that the glasses are recording audio. Wearable devices like Bee’s Pioneer emit a light to indicate they are recording, though the device is so obscure that most people may still not realize.
“The user should disclose to the room that the recording is in progress, as it is required by any other recording device,” wrote a Halliday media contact in response to questions from WIRED.
The G2s are the second iteration of Halliday’s glasses. The company introduced its first pair at CES 2025, which received mixed reviews and wound up in the “Don’t Bother” category of WIRED’s smart glasses guide. They have also garnered criticism on sites like Reddit and had to field lots of frustration on the original Kickstarter-backed version of its device. Halliday is back for round two, aiming to boost the specs—and the price—of its previous offering. The G2 glasses are aimed squarely at “high-performance professionals” like founders, CEOs, or really anyone with enough disposable cash to cop a pair of $600 glasses for their meetings.
The glasses have a display field toward the top of the lens, meaning the wearer can look up to see text on the screen. Microphones embedded in the frame listen to what’s happening nearby and can translate spoken language into text subtitles right in the wearer’s field of vision. It’s a handy use case that, in theory, can be a great tool for helping hard-of-hearing or deaf people capture conversations. Halliday says the display can also handle translation in 45 languages and notifications for messages and phone calls.
Halliday’s focus for its G2 glasses is on the meeting room. Like a bevy of other AI-powered note-taking devices, the goal is to have a device that can listen in and track all the details your coworkers are going on about.
It’s powered by the company’s AI recording and transcription service, called Meeting Flow. The mics on the glasses listen in on a meeting, and then the AI helps organize and summarize what people are saying. Some of those insights will pop up on the display so the wearer can see them mid-meeting. After the meeting ends, Meeting Flow aims to summarize, transcribe, and pull out what it figures are the most pertinent topics from the conversation.
Halliday says the AI is specifically focused on the important bits of a meeting, keeping track of the topics even if people wander off course. Features called Thread Tracker, Decision Confirmation, and Commitment Check aim to sort the useful stuff into an overall view of what was said. Full transcripts and post-meeting summaries are available in a companion app.
There are features built into the device to make it blend into the background, like a “Stealth mode” that automatically reduces the display’s light in dark rooms so as not to distract the wearer or others around. A teleprompter mode called Cheatsheet keeps bullet-point-style reminders of what the AI deems important details of your day on the screen for easy access. (Anduril founder Palmer Luckey has said he has used a similar function in Even Realities’ G2 glasses to help him stay on track during a TED talk.)
The smart glasses market is getting more refined, with smaller companies entering the second iteration of their product lifecycles. They’re aiming to establish some foothold before the giant tech companies, like Samsung, Google, and Apple, move in and sweep up most of the market.

title: 8 Best Smartwatches (2026): Apple, Google, and Hybrid Watches
summary: These WIRED-tested wearables reduce your reliance on a phone while keeping you connected.
full_text:
The Best Smartwatches, Backed by Years of Testing
Featured in this article
A great timepiece doesn’t just display the time of day. It can also elevate your outfit and make you feel good. The best smartwatches can do even more, from tracking your workouts and heart rate to serving as a notification hub and accessing voice assistants. While wearing a connected watch, you can leave your phone in your pocket and use your wrist for simple tasks.
Like many consumer gadgets today, smartwatches have gotten pricier, driven by several factors, including rising component costs and supply chain pressures. That said, the Apple Watch Series 11 remains my favorite for iPhone owners, but Google’s Pixel Watch 4 is the best smartwatch for Android users. I also like several other options—in various styles and with different levels of smarts.
Below is a roundup of the best smartwatches I’ve tested. Looking for a fitness tracker or smart ring instead? There's plenty more in our Best Fitness Trackers, Best Smart Rings, and Best Cheap Watches guides.
Updated July 2026: We've refined our recommendations and removed discontinued products; added an FAQ section and smartwatch comparison table; and updated product information, prices, and links.
Compare Top 8 Smartwatches
More Smartwatches to Consider
The number of smartwatches on the market is staggering. Here are a few other options we like.
Casio Pro Trek PRG-340B for $220: I enjoyed wearing this Casio watch—designed for the outdoors—in decidedly non-outdoor conditions for several months. From the green case to the plant-derived Castlon green strap, it looks smart and works with various outfits, even for city slickers. I largely relied on the timekeeping (in several time zones) and the stopwatch during workouts, but you can also monitor barometric pressure, altitude, and temperature, plus check the compass to get your bearings. The LCD is easy to read, and I like the auto LED function that lights up the screen when you tilt the watch. Best of all, this is a Tough Solar watch, so you won't have to bother with a charging cable. It doesn't do heart rate and notifications, but the small feature set makes this Casio useful and slightly smarter than your average timepiece. —Julian Chokkattu
Casio CA53W-1CR Calculator Watch for $40: It's a calculator on a watch. The buttons might be tiny, but you can calculate how much your tip will be when grabbing the bill at the restaurant, and everyone will marvel at your brilliance. This cheapo watch from Casio is a classic—it's comfy and lightweight—and you can cycle through a few modes, including a stopwatch, an alarm, and a second time zone. There's a five-year battery life, and the fully automatic calendar goes through the year 2099 (that's 15 battery changes). If you're interested in non-smartwatches, check out our Best Cheap Watches Under $1,000 guide. —Julian Chokkattu
Casio G-Shock Master of G Rangeman GPR-H1000 for $520: It's not for every event, but the Master of G-Land Rangeman (GPRH1000RY1A) looks great on my wrist, and I love that I only need to charge it about once a week. This is a G-Shock first and foremost. It has a durable, thick case and a comfortable strap. It's a big watch. It also has six sensors and a built-in GPS. Connect the watch to your smartphone via Casio's app, and you can get simple notification alerts, heart-rate tracking, activity tracking, and sleep tracking. That's without mentioning other features like blood oxygen monitoring, compass, world time, altimeter, and barometer. I've compared the results to an Apple Watch Series 10, and for the most part, core metrics like heart rate, step tracking, and sleep stages are similar. I have had some data not show up in the Casio app for a few days, and many of these functions are slow to load on the watch. This would not be my first choice if I wanted a fitness-focused wearable—get a Garmin instead—but I like the ability to look at and track some of these metrics whenever I want. —Julian Chokkattu
Withings ScanWatch 2 for $370: The ScanWatch 2 has been on the market for several years now—one of the few analog smartwatches that discreetly offers a robust suite of health-tracking features. While Withings has introduced new versions of it in fresh styles (like the Nova), the hardware is largely the same. In the fall of 2025, Withings released a new operating system called HealthSense 4, and you don't need to buy a new ScanWatch 2 to receive it. The health-tracking algorithms are more accurate, there are more predictive features, and you even get longer battery life (35 days). I retested the ScanWatch 2, and overall, I enjoyed my time with it; the data is laid out nicely in the Withings app. The tiny display is still a problem, but I can get the gist of incoming-message notifications, and it's easy to scroll with the crown to quickly glance at heart rate, steps, sleep data, and even start a workout. What is frustrating is that any semblance of insight into your data is paywalled behind the Withings+ subscription ($8 per month or $99 a year). My sleep data was more accurate on the Apple Watch and Pixel Watch 4, though the other metrics are on point. If you want a nice-looking analog watch to track basic health data, the ScanWatch 2 is solid, but I think it's time for fresh hardware. —Julian Chokkattu
Apple Watch Series 10 for $360: Thanks to watchOS 27, the 2024 Series 10 has many of the same features as the new Series 11, like hypertension notifications and Sleep Score. It has a thinner and lighter design with a larger screen than prior models, and it even got blood oxygen sensing back via a software update in August 2025. It's too bad this one still has the 18-hour battery life. Avoid paying anywhere close to MSRP for this watch. If you can find it for under $300, snag it. —Boutayna Chokrane
Apple Watch Ultra 2 for $730: The Watch Ultra 2 is still worth considering, just don't pay anywhere near MSRP; otherwise, you may as well buy the new Watch Ultra 3. It can last several days of use, and has many of the same great features as the latest model, including better mics to pick up your voice, an 86-decibel siren to alert your position to anyone nearby, and precise GPS to better track your hikes (plus help you find your way back with the Backtrack feature). The screen can display topographic maps, but you cannot view offline maps without an iPhone. —Boutayna Chokrane
Google Pixel Watch 3 for $300: The Pixel Watch 3 is seeing some steep discounts now that the Pixel Watch 4 is here. It's a great smartwatch, with the caveat that it's not repairable. (The newer model addresses that.) It features loss-of-pulse detection—cleared by the FDA for use in the US—which can be critical in saving someone’s life. Google also focused its fitness updates on running, enabling users to create custom runs and follow AI-powered run recommendations while getting feedback on cardio load—how hard your heart is working and whether it's appropriate for your body. I strongly recommend you go with the 45-mm model, which doesn't even feel that big. It simply delivers better battery life—just about 24 hours with the always-on display or a little more if you have it turned off. —Julian Chokkattu
Samsung's Galaxy Watch Ultra 2025 for $650: The 47-mm Galaxy Watch Ultra is the company's Apple Watch Ultra and Garmin competitor, and it's a solid first entry into the world of pricey, feature-rich, and powerful smartwatches designed for professional athletes. This is technically the 2025 model, which is identical to the 2024 version but comes with 64 GB of storage and in a new blue color. It lasts a little over two days on a charge because it's a big 47-mm watch and can pack a beefy battery. There's a titanium case and sapphire glass face, plus it's rated to 10 ATM and IP68, so you can submerge it underwater to 100 meters. title: The Best Smart Home Accessories to Boost Your Curb Appeal (2026)
summary: These locks, lights, and other smart home upgrades let you add automation without messing up your home’s vibe.
full_text:
The days are longer, the weather's warming up, and we're all spending more time outdoors. I certainly am as my son begs to ride his bike to the playground every day after school now that the sun hasn't immediately set.
As we transition into these longer days, you might find yourself looking to solve a few problems for your outdoor-living lifestyle. Maybe you want to upgrade to a smart lock to make it easier to hang out in the neighborhood without needing to worry about your keys or locking the front door, or maybe you want some fun lighting that you don't need to manually turn on and off. Either way, those problems and many more can be solved by all kinds of outdoor smart home gadgets. Smart locks, smart lights, and more can upgrade your outdoor lounging and hosting experience from now until daylight savings sneaks up on us again.
But not every piece of smart home gear is easy on the eyes. If you're big on curb appeal, these are the gadgets I recommend grabbing to give your home some smarts without costing you in the style department.
Updated July 2026: I added the BeatBot AquaSense 2 for yards that have pools, and ensured up-to-date links and prices.
A Discreet Smart Lock
I am obsessed with this smart lock. The Level Lock Pro is a full-lock replacement, but it looks like you kept the original front of your lock and only swapped out the backing (which is also an option! More on invisible swaps below.) The inside even looks normal, unlike the massive, bulky backing most smart locks have. The only one who will know it's smart is you.
Even with such a small form, it's not lacking in features. You'll get lots of unlocking options, including NFC and Apple Home Key, plus Matter compatibility and a long battery life. You'll want to add Level's Connect Wi-Fi Bridge ($79) if you want to control it from afar.
A Sleek Doorbell
When I think of a video doorbell I actually want on my home, the Nest Doorbell is the one I think of. The stylish form factor feels like a big upgrade from the bulky shapes of the Ring camera, and it comes in a handful of finishes to best match your home. It is still obvious what it is, but all video doorbells are; this one is the least amount of eyesore.
I tried the battery version, which does require you recharge it every couple of weeks, but the wired-in version is the top recommendation on our guide to the Best Video Doorbells.
A Better Birdhouse
I had a new-to-me problem this spring: bird invasion. A little bird made a nest in my front-door wreath without us noticing. One evening, my sister opened the door, and the bird flew out of the nest and straight into our house. After a 30-minute battle to get it outside again (and keep my cat from eating it), it wasn't until we saw the bird fly off the door again the next day that we realized it was calling our home its home, too.
If this is a common problem at your house, our resident bird-gear tester Kat Merck has a solution: a smart nesting box. Birdfy makes a few different smart bird feeders we like for bird-watching, and the Nest Duo is a birdhouse that lets you watch the birds while they nest inside of it. It's a slim, attractive box that will add to your front yard's style while also packing two solar-powered cameras (one facing the entrance, one focused inside) so you can bird-watch from multiple angles. It comes with different hole sizes to appeal to different species, metal predator guards to prevent chewing around the hole, and a remote control to reset or recharge the camera without disturbing your feathered neighbors.
Stylish Smart Lights
I've liked Govee's smart outdoor string lights before, usually for my holiday decor, and have previously recommended something similar with a bistro-light-like look that happened to be smart. These clear bulb string lights are part of Govee's current lineup and have a contemporary twist with a triangle in the center instead of the wire filament. These are a fun option for outdoor lights you can enjoy on warm nights, and they can do every color and shade of white without looking as bulky as permanent outdoor lights. (Added bonus, these lights are also Matter compatible!)
Fresh Bulbs
If you have light fixtures you want to remote-control, add an outdoor smart bulb. There are tons to choose from, and you can usually find one from any brand you already have at home. The only downside is that outdoor-rated smart bulbs are usually 4.75-inch-diameter PAR38-style bulbs, so they're best for downward-facing floodlights on your porch or balcony. They'll likely be too big to fit in a wall fixture as a replacement for a normal-sized bulb. Don't just grab any smart bulb—not all are outdoor-rated. Check for mentions of outdoor use and waterproof ratings to make sure they're safe to use. I'm a big fan of Cync bulbs, and the brand has an outdoor version of the Cync Full Color bulbs I like to use indoors. You'll be able to add fun colors as well as shades of white, so you can turn the porch a spooky orange or red for Halloween, pink for Valentine's Day, or the colors of your favorite sports team on game day.
A Clean Pool
I'll never forget the gorgeous Airbnb I stayed at once that had a pool right in the front yard. Most pools aren't really something you need to worry about for official curb appeal, but if you can spot your pool from anywhere outside of your home, you'll want it looking pristine. My parents’ pool was one you could see from the road behind their house, for example, and while we didn't have that many trees, it still needed a ton of cleaning. If you're sick of trying to keep your pool clean, there's a handy gadget that can help: a robotic pool cleaner. It's like a robot vacuum but for your pool, working autonomously to scrub the floors, walls, and waterline. Beatbot makes a few different robot pool cleaners we like, but WIRED reviewer Christopher Null says the AquaSense 2 is a great option for under $1,000. It has three cleaning modes and a run time of four hours, and will return to its docking station to wirelessly recharge after it cleans.
Remote-Controlled Garage
If your garage is the centerpiece of your home's curb appeal, you can control it as easily as a smart door by adding a smart controller. You can do two different styles: I have the Chamberlain MyQ professionally installed smart garage opener, which means the device that controls my garage has these smarts built into it (plus a camera, but I find it doesn't work great with how far the device is from my Wi-Fi router), or you can get a smart garage controller that can add smart features onto an existing garage door. Both let you check whether the garage is open or closed and operate it remotely, and you can add a video keypad that doubles as a video doorbell and can let you open or close the garage without your phone.
Smart Shades
The front of my home faces west, so it's absolutely baking at the end of the day. What I need to add are some of our favorite smart shades to automate closing the shades on that side of the house at the right time of day. These also give your home a nice, cohesive look and immediate, controllable privacy from the outside world. WIRED reviewer Simon Hill recommends the SmartWings shades as his top picks, and Lutron's Caseta shades if you're looking for a more upgraded look.
Invisible Swaps
Looking to add some smarts without touching your existing setup? These switch-ups can make your front door and yard smart without being visible.

title: Abdul El-Sayed Is an Epidemiologist Running for Senate. His State Is a Public Health Disaster
summary: Michigan has been at the epicenter of the wildfire smoke and explosive diarrhea outbreaks. The progressive Democrat talks to WIRED about how he would tackle the forces behind them if he’s elected.
full_text:
Michigan is ground zero for the twin public health crises wreaking havoc in the US. The state has had some of the most polluted air on Earth due to Canadian wildfire smoke last week while it also has the highest number of cyclosporiasis cases in the country.
These in-your-face (and sometimes in-your-gut) problems, says senatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed, help make a complex topic—the need to invest in public health infrastructure—extremely easy to talk about with voters. And he has unique qualifications to do so as a MD-PhD who’s served as the health officer for Detroit.
“Do you like eating lettuce? I do. I don’t like the idea because we DOGE’d our whole service that keeps the lettuce safe,” El-Sayed says, referring to how the Department of Government Efficiency downsized the federal lab that tests for cyclosporiasis last year. “Now, everybody’s trying to dodge the lettuce. And if you don’t, then you’re stuck on a toilet for the next five days. That sucks.”
El-Sayed is locked in a tight Democratic primary for Michigan’s open senatorial seat. He’s received support from big-name progressives: Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez rallied with him in Grand Rapids over the weekend, while Senator Elizabeth Warren endorsed him on Monday. In her endorsement, Warren said El-Sayed was someone who would fight “the same billionaires and special interests that have rigged our economy against working people.” For El-Sayed, that includes addressing election spending.
“A lot of this, in the end, comes back to getting money out of politics,” he says. “A lot of these changes in regulations are about massive food companies being like, well, those regulations are too much. We can enforce them ourselves. I’m like, can you? How come you didn’t fix the poop lettuce?”
WIRED caught up with El-Sayed to chat about how he’d fix the public health problems facing his state and why we shouldn’t accept that “poop lettuce” is our new normal.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
WIRED: How have the past few weeks been for you personally, with this one-two punch of public health crises?
Abdul El-Sayed: I don’t know what happened, but for four days I got taken out—I didn’t get tested, because I was on the campaign trail, but I think it was [cyclosporiasis]. If you can imagine campaigning, it was miserable. It was actually my wife who was like, you probably got this.
And then for the past week or so, we’ve been really worried about air quality. I try to stay active—I do a lot of biking—and I’ve been choosing to stay inside. You do more harm than good exercising outside with this kind of air quality.
You shouldn’t have to be dodging lettuce everywhere you go and then unknowingly getting the runs because you didn’t dodge the lettuce. Step back and ask yourself if any of this is normal.
You’ve had a lot of experience handling crises like these at the local and state level. What would you do in the Senate, especially given an administration that has been taking away funding and staff and the basic tools of public health, like peer-reviewed science and public data?
I’d love to be able to haul up leaders at the EPA, the CDC, and the FDA [to testify before Congress]. I want to investigate exactly how our food supply got compromised, how decisions were made at the CDC. Why are their counts so far behind? For the vast majority of people, cyclosporiasis is not a deadly outcome—but imagine what happens when the same infrastructure has to deal with something that really is. What are we going to do then?
There are certain things that you should take for granted: that you can eat food and stay generally healthy, or that you can breathe the air and go outside without that making you sick. You think about the great DOGEing of a lot of our public health infrastructure—while it’s impossible to connect one outcome to the next, if you cut the staff of the people who are supposed to be invested in keeping us healthy, don’t be surprised when, down the line, they’re not good at keeping us healthy. Now, we’re dealing with the consequences.
When DOGE was happening, it would have been really important to have had a public health senator, who could ask the hard questions about what they’re dismantling, and if they even know the broader functions of the things they’re dismantling.
Both the outbreak and the wildfire smoke seem to me to be very visceral symptoms of larger, really thorny issues—climate change, disinvestment in public health, modern corporatization of food systems—that are tough to get voters invested in solving. How do you talk to people about systemic issues like these?
The hard part about these problems is that they operate on very long time horizons. Too often the conversation is more about these petty, esoteric questions—about the competence of the public health infrastructure, or 2 degrees centigrade—rather than, hey, kids shouldn’t have asthma and you should stop putting pollution in the air.
People don’t want to be stuck on a toilet for the better part of the day, every day. That means we have to keep our food clean and track when this happens, so that if we do have something that’s a deadly disease next time, we have the public health infrastructure ready to go. We could get better, more reliable jobs if we actually just invested in renewable energy. If we were serious about the energy transition that we need to have, we can create a massive number of union jobs.
I’m glad you brought up renewable energy. Michigan is ground zero for anti-renewables sentiment: It has the highest level of anti-solar and anti-wind ordinances in the country. How do you meet voters where they are on issues like these, where they might be resistant to some of the things that we need to do to address systemic problems?
At the end of the day, the big challenge that people across my state are experiencing is not climate change writ large. It’s “I can’t afford to pay my rent. I’m really worried about whether or not I’ll ever have a home. I’m really worried about what happens if I see a doctor, and that damn utility company keeps raising my rates, and now they’re trying to charge me extra money just to pay my bills.”
It behooves us to be talking about those problems, because those are the problems everyday people are facing. When you take those problems and build them out, you start to realize that they are part and parcel of a whole bigger set of problems that are really important for everyday people’s lives, but just aren’t the imminent problems that everybody is facing today. I think it’s important for us to be constantly talking about the challenges people face, because those are the real things people want us to solve, but also connecting them to the bigger picture. We can have these conversations, but we’ve got to make sure people understand the full burden of the issue.
If you’re elected, you’ll be entering a Congress that seems to get more and more dysfunctional each year. Some Republicans are now recommending sanctioning Canada over the wildfire smoke.
[Laughs] It’s so unserious. We’ve got to be able to be like, what you’re saying is laughably ridiculous. The problem with the Democrats is that we’re so afraid of our own shadow, we actually don’t make any arguments.
I’m wondering if you have any hope of working across the aisle on literally anything, or having productive conversations with politicians across the aisle.
There’s a more important conversation between all of us and the people who elect us. I’ve been traveling up and down my state talking to folks who don’t always think like me on the issues, and both learning how they’re thinking about things, and how we solve their problems.
I think I can build some really good bipartisan relationships with folks who voted on the other side. Do you really want to be breathing this stuff right now? Do you really want to be dodging lettuce? I don’t think anyone wants to be dodging lettuce. Seems to be a pretty bipa

title: ‘It’s a Modern-Day Draft’: Why Stanford Students Walked Out on Sundar Pichai’s Commencement Speech
summary: Last month, more than a hundred Stanford students left their own graduation to protest Google’s military contracts and deals with ICE. Two organizers, Amanda Campos and Eva Jones, tell us why.
full_text:
Are the kids all right? The answer to that question probably depends on your criteria. At the very least, I can tell you that some of them are most definitely very mad.
The anger percolating among America’s youth was on display this graduation season, as college students across the country booed and jeered several high-profile commencement speakers who dared discuss—let alone extol the benefits of—artificial intelligence. While AI use among college kids is widespread, so too is the fear and mistrust about what the technology might mean for the future. A recent Gallup poll found that Gen Z sentiment toward AI has significantly declined, with only 22 percent of respondents expressing excitement about the tech—and anxiety around AI affecting 42 percent of them.
Among the commencement speech chaos, though, one school stood out to me: Stanford University. The California-based institution, long a key hub for Silicon Valley recruiting and a pipeline into elite tech gigs, this year saw more than a hundred students walk out of Google CEO Sundar Pichai’s remarks to graduates. Ironically, Pichai didn’t explicitly mention AI in his address at all. But for the organizers of the Stanford walkout, AI is only a tangential concern: More than any specific technology, their demonstration was designed to raise awareness of Google’s contracts with the US and Israeli governments, as well as ICE.
The walkout organizers may not have convinced Google to change its ways, but they did manage to create an international news event. Media outlets including CNN and the BBC ran with the story, and videos of the walkout have amassed millions of views online. I wanted to know more about how the coordinated effort came to be, what student organizers hoped to accomplish, and how it feels to be newly graduating—from a school as Silicon Valley–aligned as Stanford, no less—into a world that’s now arguably run by Big Tech.
Two of the Stanford walkout organizers, Eva Jones and Amanda Campos, traveled to New York and sat down with me in person earlier this month. Our conversation is below.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
KATIE DRUMMOND: Eva Jones and Amanda Campos—welcome, both of you.
AMANDA CAMPOS: Thank you so much, Katie. Thank you for having us.
I'm delighted that you're here. Thank you for making the trip. First of all, congratulations on graduating. What did you study in school? Why did you choose Stanford four years ago when you were thinking about where to go to undergrad?
Campos: I studied environmental policy at Stanford, and I am currently working in the environmental justice activism and advocacy space in California.
I quite literally came to Stanford because I knew I wanted to take action, to solve the environmental crisis. I grew up in Brazil, and since I was little it was the huge issue I saw as being able to take action towards.
But arriving at Stanford, I quickly realized [the school] just had so much fossil fuel money and bias, and I quickly became an organizer as a result. As a sophomore, when October 2023 came, I quite quickly realized how intertwined the environmental justice movement and the movement for Palestinian liberation are.
It goes back to the corporate ties Stanford has, and choosing a Google CEO is indicative of such a tie and of such a bias, really. I was a lead organizer with Stanford SJP, Students for Justice in Palestine, and as soon as we heard about Sundar Pichai being chosen as the commencement speaker, we knew we had to do something.
Eva, what about you? What did you go to Stanford to study?
EVA JONES: I am a recent graduate, having studied hydrology and water resources for my master’s degree, but I also did my bachelor’s programs there, in feminist philosophy and in freshwater engineering.
I came to Stanford five years ago now, from a rural town in Oregon, because I truly believed that a place like Stanford was looking to pool together minds and resources to tackle these existential threats to humanity, to build the kind of world that I always envisioned could be possible, one of connection, one of belonging.
I'm curious, Amanda, you talked about how you got involved with student organizing to begin with, but I'd love to hear from both of you a little bit more about that. How did you go from student to campus activist and organizer?
Jones: I came to Stanford as a student organizer. I was of the generation of students who were part of climate justice organizing, anti-gun-violence things, people who came into university ready to use their voice, thinking of that as a way to build a future.
As soon as I got to Stanford, I got involved in anti-sexual violence organizing, which quickly put me in opposition with the administration.
By 2023, when the student encampments in solidarity with Palestine began, that was something that we saw so many more students get involved in and really come together to build something more than just opposition. But more broadly, I did come in also a bit naive in terms of thinking about Stanford as this place where I can innovate on environmental solutions, where I can help people.
I saw the power of education, the power of a Stanford degree as a way to do that. But I think my view of power has definitely changed, especially through organizing. I viewed power as something to gain, and now I view it as something to build, as something that we all have through our voices.
Getting involved in SJP organizing, for me, has been extremely liberating. I have a lot of hope in the student movement.

It describes Stanford as basically what you are both saying, a funnel into tech jobs and Silicon Valley, a place with a lot of clubbiness, tech elitism, VCs scouting for talent, and plenty of ethical lapses on the part of students and faculty and administration. Do you have any reactions to that book?

I think it really distracts from the actual issues going on, which are, in many ways, defense-propelled career pipelines at these universities and in Silicon Valley, at these companies that run deep and fuel really violent technologies and systems of control.

title: Jack Mallers Steps Down as Twenty One Capital CEO as Tether Merger Unravels
summary:
The Strike founder is leaving the Tether-controlled treasury company after a board disagreement, as a proposed three-way merger with Strike and Elektron Energy collapses.

The post Jack Mallers Steps Down as Twenty One Capital CEO as Tether Merger Unravels appeared first on Unchained.
full_text:
Bitcoin financial-services company Strike founder Jack Mallers has stepped down as chief executive of Twenty One Capital, the Tether-controlled treasury company he helped launch. In a video statement posted to X, Mallers said he had decided to leave to return to Strike.
Mallers tied his departure to a disagreement over direction, saying that over time “the board and I did not agree on the path toward building for that vision.” He described the split as amicable, saying no one had acted in bad faith.
Twenty One said its board appointed Raphael Zagury, founder and chief executive of Bitcoin miner Elektron Energy and an existing company director, as CEO effective July 20. Zagury and Mallers are working together on an orderly transition, Twenty One said.
Tether’s Three-Way Merger Falls Apart
The leadership change came alongside confirmation that Strike is pulling out of Tether Investments’ proposed three-way merger folding Twenty One, Strike, and Elektron into a single listed platform spanning treasury, mining, financial services, and capital markets. Twenty One now says Strike will stay independent and is off the table as a merger partner. A two-way tie-up with Elektron stays under evaluation but at a preliminary stage, with no assurance it closes.
Twenty One, meanwhile, outlined a refreshed strategy centered on operating businesses, disciplined capital allocation, and Bitcoin-backed lending.
“My job is to build the operating company around it, with the discipline, governance, and executional rigor of an institution,” Zagury said in a statement shared by Twenty One. “I believe our business will perform best when we also focus on the cash flow we generate and the rigor with which we allocate capital, not only by the Bitcoin we hold.”

title: Google 推出 Gemini 3.6 Flash 等三款新模型！3.5 Flash-Lite 飆出極速，Gemini 4 預訓練已啟動
summary:
據 Google 官方部落格公告，Google 於 21 日正式推出新一代 Flash 系列模型，包含 Gem […]

〈Google 推出 Gemini 3.6 Flash 等三款新模型！3.5 Flash-Lite 飆出極速，Gemini 4 預訓練已啟動〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
據 Google 官方部落格公告，Google 於 21 日正式推出新一代 Flash 系列模型，包含 Gemini 3.6 Flash、3.5 Flash-Lite 以及 3.5 Flash Cyber。新模型專為 AI 代理（AI agents）工作流打造，不僅大幅降低輸出成本與代幣消耗，更內建了強大的電腦操作能力，全面劍指企業級的大規模生產部署。
（前情提要：Google 傳推出全新「frozen」晶片效能狂飆 10 倍！Alphabet 市值暴增 1150 億鎂）
（背景補充：Gemini 3.5 Pro 難產數月：Google 政治派系內鬥讓員工備感挫折）
隨著人工智慧（AI）技術邁入代理化（Agentic）時代，大型語言模型在速度、成本與推理能力上的平衡，已成為企業採用的關鍵考量。台北時間 2026 年 7 月 21 日，Google 團隊產品管理資深總監 Tulsee Doshi 發表官方文章，宣布推出基於先前用戶反饋所打造的三款全新 Flash 系列模型，進一步鞏固其在 AI 代理領域的基礎設施優勢。
Gemini 3.6 Flash：效能大躍進，輸出成本更低
作為新一代的主力工作模型，Gemini 3.6 Flash 在程式碼編寫、知識工作與多模態任務上的表現獲得了顯著提升。數據顯示，該模型在電腦使用能力評測（OSWorld-Verified）中達到了 83.0% 的高分，且相關的電腦使用工具現已直接內建於 Gemini API 與企業版中。
此外，3.6 Flash 大幅優化了代幣（Token）的使用效率。根據 Artificial Analysis Index 顯示，其輸出代幣使用量比前代減少了 17%，在某些基準測試（如 DeepSWE）中最高甚至可減少 65%。這不僅減少了多步驟工作流的推理與工具呼叫時間，也讓定價更具競爭力 —— 輸入為每百萬代幣 1.50 美元，輸出為 7.50 美元。
3.5 Flash-Lite：極致輕量化，飆出 350 tokens/s 高速
針對需要低延遲與高吞吐量的任務（例如代理搜尋與文件處理），Google 推出了專屬的 Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite。該模型的輸出速度高達每秒 350 個代幣，且輸入成本極低，僅需每百萬代幣 0.3 美元（輸出為 2.5 美元）。
儘管定位為輕量級，3.5 Flash-Lite 的品質卻遠超先前的 Lite 世代。其支援可調整的「思考級別（thinking levels）」，讓開發者能在低思考模式與處理複雜子代理工作流的高思考模式之間自由切換。在長上下文與代理編碼評測中，它甚至超越了標準版的 Gemini 3 Flash 模型。
專攻網路安全，Gemini 4 預訓練已啟動
在本次更新中，Google 也針對特定的安全防禦場景，發布了基於 3.5 Flash 微調的「Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber」模型。該模型能搭配多代理系統 CodeMender 協作產生綜合報告，協助防禦者快速發現並修復網路安全漏洞。然而，考量到這類技術的雙重用途風險，目前僅限政府機構與受信任的合作夥伴透過試點計畫進行有限存取。
Doshi 在文末也預告，除了正與合作夥伴測試即將廣泛推出的 Gemini 3.5 Pro 外，Google 目前已正式啟動了 Gemini 4 的預訓練工作，並形容這是該公司「最雄心勃勃」的計畫。即日起，開發者已可透過 Gemini API 等管道存取全新的 3.6 Flash 與 3.5 Flash-Lite 模型，搶先體驗 AI 代理工作流的強大潛力。

title: 月之暗面 Moonshot AI 傳啟動 IPO 前最終融資！估值直逼 500 億美元、最快今年香港掛牌上市
summary:
據《Bloomberg》報導，中國人工智慧獨角獸 Moonshot AI（月之暗面）正計畫於 8 月展開 IP […]

〈月之暗面 Moonshot AI 傳啟動 IPO 前最終融資！估值直逼 500 億美元、最快今年香港掛牌上市〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
據《Bloomberg》報導，中國人工智慧獨角獸 Moonshot AI（月之暗面）正計畫於 8 月展開 IPO 前的最終輪融資，目標估值高達 500 億美元，最快有望於今年內在香港掛牌上市。受惠於近期發布號稱全球最大的開放權重模型 Kimi K3，該公司 6 月年度經常性收入（ARR）已飆升至 3 億美元，商業化進展驚人。
（前情提要：擠爆！Kimi K3 上線 48 小時用量達上限，月之暗面暫停新訂閱）
（背景補充：月之暗面 Moonshot AI 即將推出 Kimi K3！具備 2.8 兆參數與百萬長文本，性能直逼 Anthropic Opus 4.8）
隨著人工智慧技術的商業化步伐加快，頂尖 AI 新創正迎來資本市場的狂歡。台北時間 2026 年 7 月 21 日，據《Bloomberg》引述知情人士的獨家報導指出，中國 AI 領軍企業 Moonshot AI（月之暗面）正積極籌備進入公開市場，其募資速度與規模皆令業界矚目。
估值衝上 500 億美元，加速拆除紅籌架構
報導披露，Moonshot AI 目前正在收尾今年夏天啟動的一輪融資，該輪估值已達 315 億美元，預計將於近日內正式完成。更震撼的是，公司計畫在該輪完成後，立即於 8 月展開與投資人的「最後一輪融資」談判，目標估值將一舉推升至高達 500 億美元。
這筆巨額資金預計將成為該公司首次公開發行（IPO）前的最後一次資金注入。消息來源指出，Moonshot AI 的目標是最快於今年內在香港掛牌上市。為了替境內融資與 IPO 鋪路，公司目前正加速拆除海外紅籌架構，相關重組作業預計將在本月底前完成。
Kimi K3 震撼市場，性能直逼 OpenAI
支撐起這驚人估值躍升的關鍵，是該公司近期在技術上的重大突破。上週，Moonshot AI 正式發表了旗下最新模型 Kimi K3。這款號稱全球最大「開放權重（open-weight）」的 AI 模型，據稱擁有高達 28 億億的驚人參數規模。
業界評估指出，Kimi K3 的性能表現已相當接近 OpenAI 與 Anthropic 等美國巨頭的最新前沿模型。這項技術里程碑不僅大幅翻轉了外界對於「中國 AI 發展嚴重落後美國」的刻板印象，也成為吸引國際投資人高度關注、促使公司趁勢快速募資的核心催化劑。這對於年僅 33 歲、曾任職於 Meta 與 Google 的低調卡內基梅隆大學校友 —— 創辦人楊植麟（Yang Zhilin）而言，無疑是一次巨大的成功與肯定。
商業化進展迅猛，ARR 突破 3 億美元
在技術實力獲得認可的同時，Moonshot AI 的變現能力同樣令人驚豔。根據《Bloomberg》揭露的數據，該公司在今年 6 月的年度經常性收入（ARR）已成功達到 3 億美元，相較於 4 月時的 2 億美元，呈現出極為陡峭的成長曲線。
此外，自 Kimi K3 模型推出以來，公司的每日銷售額至少實現了 6 倍的爆發性成長。這種在熱門領域取得技術突破後，迅速將流量轉化為營收，並以遠超美國同業的速度推進資本化進程的策略，正充分展現了中國科技新創從私募走向公開市場的強大爆發力。截至目前，Moonshot AI 官方尚未對上述融資與 IPO 傳聞做出正式回應。

通訊軟體巨頭 Telegram 創辦人 Pavel Durov 今（21）日宣布，今年夏天將為全球用戶推出原生 […]

〈Telegram 宣布內建非託管錢包！$GRAM 10 分鐘狂飆 9% 突破 1.5 美元〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
通訊軟體巨頭 Telegram 創辦人 Pavel Durov 今（21）日宣布，今年夏天將為全球用戶推出原生、非託管的 Gram 錢包，預告這將是人類史上最大規模的錢包部署。受此重磅利多激勵，GRAM 代幣價格在 10 分鐘內暴漲超 9%，強勢突破 1.5 美元大關。
（前情提要：Telegram 短網域 t.me 連結遭註冊方停用！創辦人 Pavel Durov 也無預警）
（背景補充：讓 AI 自己溝通！Telegram 開放「Bot-to-Bot」機器人對話，但必須嚴防這一問題）
通訊軟體巨頭 Telegram 在加密貨幣領域的佈局迎來歷史性進展。台北時間 7 月 21 日，Telegram 創辦人 Pavel Durov 在其個人頻道拋出震撼彈，宣布將於今年夏天進行「人類史上最大規模的非託管加密貨幣錢包部署」。
10 億用戶享零手續費，全面內建 Gram 錢包
Durov 在貼文中強調，未來的願景是讓全球超過 10 億用戶能夠體驗即時、零手續費的加密貨幣交易，並預告這一切即將成為現實。
他進一步明確指出：「我們將為每一個 Telegram 應用程式帶來原生的非託管 Gram 錢包！」這意味著 Telegram 龐大的用戶群未來將能直接在 App 內完全掌控自己的加密資產，無須再依賴第三方的中心化託管機構，進一步實踐 Web3 的去中心化精神。
GRAM 聞訊狂飆，10 分鐘暴漲逾 9%
這項重磅宣示大幅提振了市場對 Telegram 相關生態系的信心。在 Durov 發文後，與之緊密相關的 GRAM 代幣隨即迎來猛烈買盤。
市場數據顯示，GRAM 價格在短短 10 分鐘內暴漲超過 9%，強勢突破 1.5 美元的關鍵心理關卡。截至發稿時，GRAM 報價為 1.555 美元，市場熱度與交易量仍持續升溫，投資人正密切關注這項功能正式落地的確切時間表。

title: 金融時報：川普將重啟 10% 關稅！白宮內部爆意見分歧，憂經濟震盪重演
summary:
全球貿易戰恐再度升溫！據知名財經評論帳號 The Kobeissi Letter 引述《金融時報》突發報導指出 […]

〈金融時報：川普將重啟 10% 關稅！白宮內部爆意見分歧，憂經濟震盪重演〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
全球貿易戰恐再度升溫！據知名財經評論帳號 The Kobeissi Letter 引述《金融時報》突發報導指出，美國總統川普（Donald Trump）正準備於本週宣布對「數十個國家」徵收 10% 關稅。此舉引發了白宮顧問團隊的強烈擔憂，害怕在關鍵的期中選舉前夕重演貿易戰，進而對總體經濟造成嚴重衝擊。
（前情提要：川普祭出「100% 關稅」核彈！警告各國：敢對美企徵數位稅，將撕毀所有貿易協定）
（背景補充：歐中貿易逆差破 4000 億歐元：馬克宏拋「歐版對等關稅」應對中國商品低價傾銷）
隨著美國期中選舉的腳步逼近，全球市場可能再次面臨貿易保護主義帶來的劇烈動盪。台北時間 7 月 21 日，據擁有廣大影響力的財經評論帳號 The Kobeissi Letter 引述《金融時報》（Financial Times）的即時消息指出，美國總統川普（Donald Trump）計畫於本週宣布一項重大的貿易關稅政策。
BREAKING: President Trump is preparing to announce 10% tariffs on "dozens of countries" this week, per FT.
Details include:
1. These new tariffs come as President Trump's current 10% tariffs expire later this week
2. President Trump's advisors have reportedly warned him…
— The Kobeissi Letter (@KobeissiLetter) July 21, 2026
瞄準數十國，新關稅本週上膛
報導指出，川普政府正準備對「數十個國家」全面徵收 10% 的關稅。這項突如其來的舉動並非空穴來風，主因在於川普目前實施的 10% 關稅政策即將於本週晚些時候到期，因此新一輪關稅的宣布，被市場視為是延續其強硬貿易立場的關鍵動作。
顧問急勸阻！憂引爆經濟衝擊反噬選情
然而，這項激進的關稅計畫在白宮內部引發了不小的反彈與疑慮。據傳，川普的顧問團隊已經向他發出嚴厲警告，強烈建議不要在此刻重啟廣泛的關稅措施。顧問們主要擔心，在 2026 年關鍵的期中選舉前夕，貿然行事恐將重演當年貿易戰的經濟震盪，進而反噬美國國內的選情與總體經濟的穩定。
儘管面臨內部雜音，川普政府的強硬路線似乎並未動搖。The Kobeissi Letter 的貼文進一步揭露，除了這波 10% 的關稅外，川普政府同時還在推進其他相關調查，試圖以此作為法理基礎，賦予行政團隊未來提出「更高關稅」的合法權力。這意味著，全球供應鏈與金融市場在短期內恐將迎來更多來自華府的關稅震撼彈。

title: AI 讓員工變快，企業為何沒變強？Atlassian 揭露組織無法獲利的三大盲點
summary:
人工智慧（AI）席捲全球職場，但許多企業卻發現整體效率並未如預期般提升。據《VentureBeat》報導，At […]

〈AI 讓員工變快，企業為何沒變強？Atlassian 揭露組織無法獲利的三大盲點〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
人工智慧（AI）席捲全球職場，但許多企業卻發現整體效率並未如預期般提升。據《VentureBeat》報導，Atlassian Teamwork Lab 負責人 Dr. Molly Sands 近期在公開活動中直言，多數公司採用 AI 的方向「倒過來了」，只專注優化個人效率而忽略了團隊協作，導致組織難以看見實質的投資報酬率（ROI）。她強調，成功的團隊必須建立共享情境、重新設計工作流程，並培養勇於實驗的企業文化。
（前情提要：數學界 Jacobian 猜想遭證偽，OpenAI 研究員：Codex「無網路輔助」也算出來了）
（背景補充：自託管 AI 模型更省錢？Cline 實測 Kimi K3 成本優勢，網反駁：按任務算比 Fable 5 貴）
隨著生成式 AI 工具的普及，許多員工的日常作業速度確實獲得了顯著提升，但這股效率紅利似乎未能順利轉化為企業整體的競爭力。台北時間 2026 年 7 月 21 日，據《VentureBeat》發布的一篇由軟體巨頭 Atlassian 贊助的報導，Atlassian Teamwork Lab 負責人 Dr. Molly Sands 在 VB Transform 2026 活動中，深刻剖析了這個看似矛盾的職場現象。
個人效率提升，組織卻不見 ROI
在這場由 VentureBeat 資深科技貢獻者 Sam Witteveen 主持的爐邊談話中，Sands 一語道破了問題的核心：大多數公司採用 AI 的方式是「倒過來的」。企業往往只專注於優化個別員工如何使用 AI，卻未將眼光放在優化團隊層級的協同工作方式。
這種失衡導致了一個尷尬的結果：雖然個人跑得更快了，但由於團隊流程未經調整，這些方向略有不同的個人反而會「很快撞在一起」，導致組織整體無法看見明顯的投資報酬率（ROI）。Sands 領導的行為科學家與心理學家團隊，不僅研究 AI 對協作的影響，更致力於實際幫助企業重新設計工作流程。
僅 6% 主管看見實際價值，成功團隊具備三大特徵
根據《Atlassian 2026 State of Teams Report》針對全球 12,000 名知識工作者，以及約 200 名 Fortune 1000 高階主管的調查，高達 89% 的主管承認公司內個人使用 AI 後速度確實變快。然而，令人訝異的是，僅有 6% 的主管能指出明確的 ROI 案例；並且，只有約 14% 的團隊成功將 AI 的使用轉化為真正的價值，顯示出即使在同一家公司內，團隊間的績效落差也極為懸殊。
Sands 指出，那些成功將 AI 轉化為團隊優勢的組織，通常具備三大共同特徵：
- 情境（Context）：成功團隊會建立「情境圖（context graph）」，將目標、決策與組織知識系統性地記錄在 Jira 或 Confluence 等共享的數位平台中，讓 AI 能取得組織層級的脈絡，而非僅依賴個人的孤立提示詞（prompt）。
- 工作流程（Workflows）：他們不只加速單一任務，而是重新設計整個端到端（end-to-end）的工作流程。
- 文化（Culture）：領導者明確鼓勵學習與實驗，並能包容實驗過程中的失敗。
制定「AI 工作協議」，暴露潛藏的組織裂痕
為了幫助企業跨越這道鴻溝，Sands 建議團隊可以透過設定刻意的限制來快速學習，例如將任務拆解至最小單位，或是挑戰「一週內完全不手寫程式碼」。此外，在專案啟動時制定明確的「AI 工作協議（AI Working Agreements）」也至關重要，這包含決定哪些事務應交由 AI 處理、哪些需迴避，以及團隊應共享哪些代理程式（agents）與技能。
文章最後帶出了一個更深層的啟示：AI 其實並未創造出全新的管理難題，它只是無情地暴露了組織內原本就存在的裂痕，例如隱藏的假設與不同的心智模型。AI 的介入放大了這些差距的後果，使得「共享情境」與「明確的工作方式」在未來的企業營運中，變得比以往任何時候都更加迫切與重要。

title: 俄羅斯國家杜馬今日決議加密貨幣法案！散戶年限買 30 萬盧布，最快 9/1 生效
summary:
俄羅斯長期的加密貨幣監管僵局即將打破。據外媒《Cointelegraph》報導，俄羅斯國家杜馬將於今（21）日 […]

〈俄羅斯國家杜馬今日決議加密貨幣法案！散戶年限買 30 萬盧布，最快 9/1 生效〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
俄羅斯長期的加密貨幣監管僵局即將打破。據外媒《Cointelegraph》報導，俄羅斯國家杜馬將於今（21）日對《關於數位貨幣和數位權利》法案進行最終審議（二讀與三讀）。該法案不僅為加密資產在跨境貿易中的合法使用鋪路，同時對一般散戶與合格投資者設定了嚴格的購買與轉帳上限。新規若順利過關，預計將於今年 9 月 1 日正式生效。
（前情提要：俄羅斯推進加密貨幣合法化：散戶每年限購 30 萬盧布，擁抱數位資產跨境結算）
（背景補充：美國警告：俄羅斯計劃對波蘭發動武裝行動，以測試北約集體防衛決心）
俄羅斯政府在面對西方嚴厲的金融制裁下，正加速構建專屬的數位資產監管體系，試圖透過加密貨幣在國際貿易中突圍。台北時間 7 月 21 日，據外媒《Cointelegraph》報導，俄羅斯國家杜馬（State Duma）將於今日針對編號 1194918-8 的《關於數位貨幣和數位權利》（On Digital Currency and Digital Rights）法案進行第二讀與第三讀的最終投票。
突破制裁封鎖，放行跨境貿易支付
多年來，俄羅斯政府內部對於如何監管加密貨幣一直爭論不休，但隨著國際金融制裁的加劇，俄國積極尋找繞過傳統金融體系的方法。這項法案的核心目的，便是為俄羅斯境內的加密貨幣活動建立一套清晰的法律框架，特別是在跨境支付與貿易應用上。
俄羅斯國家杜馬金融市場委員會主席 Anatoly Aksakov 對此表示，該法案將為加密貨幣在俄羅斯境內的合法使用創造完善的條件。值得注意的是，新規將允許向俄羅斯供應商品的外國企業與本地公司，使用加密資產進行支付結算，而不會受到過多的法律限制。事實上，近期如 Alfa-Bank 等俄羅斯大型商業銀行，也已經開始著手測試相關的加密貨幣交易服務。
嚴格投資分級：散戶年限買 30 萬盧布
儘管法案大幅放寬了企業層級的跨境結算，但為了控管境內金融風險，俄羅斯當局對一般零售市場採取了嚴格的分級限制。法案針對不同身分的投資者，設定了明確的購買與轉帳天花板。
對於「非合格投資者（一般散戶）」，法案規定其每年透過單一中介機構購買加密貨幣的上限僅為 30 萬盧布（約合 3,800 美元），且向境外轉移加密貨幣的上限被嚴格限縮在 10 萬盧布。
另一方面，針對具備專業知識與風險承擔能力的「合格投資者」，法案則給予了較大的彈性。其年度購買上限被提高至 300 萬盧布，而向境外轉移的上限也同步放寬至 100 萬盧布。
9 月有望上路，俄羅斯加密合法化邁大步
分析指出，這項法案代表著俄羅斯在長期推動加密貨幣合法化的進程中，邁出了最具實質意義的一步。市場普遍預期，在國家政策的引導下，今日的二讀與三讀投票有望順利過關。若法案如期通過，其主要條款最快將於 2026 年 9 月 1 日正式生效，屆時俄羅斯在全球加密貨幣版圖中的角色與影響力，勢必將迎來全新的轉變。
