title: How TIME and Statista Determined the World's Top EdTech Companies of 2026
summary:
TIME has published the third annual "World’s Top EdTech Companies 2026" ranking, in partnership with Statista, a leading international provider of market and consumer data and rankings. The result of this quantitative study: 500 companies dedicated to the development and provision of educational technologies, encompassing both products and services. Here's how the winners were selected.

Methodology

Main list

The research project "World's Top EdTech Companies 2026" is a comprehensive analysis conducted to identify the top performing EdTech companies in the world. First, companies had to primarily focus on developing and providing educational technologies, products or services. The 500 companies with the highest score were awarded as "World's Top EdTech Companies 2026"

The ranking is built on two pillars: financial strength and industry impact. Statista gathered and scrutinized data from around 6,500 companies through desk research, online application forms and collaborations with other data and market intelligence companies. A company received scores in each of these dimensions, which were then combined into an overall score.

For the first dimension, financial strength, Statista analyzed revenue, funding, and market capitalization data, obtained from publicly available sources like annual reports, company websites, through media monitoring, and via databases. Additionally, company disclosures submitted via an online application form, which was freely accessible via the TIME website, were considered.

For the evaluation of the industry impact, Statista cooperated with The Upright Project and LexisNexis® Intellectual Property Solutions to assess companies in different impact dimensions, encompassing factors such as:

  • holistic impact of a company’s product and service portfolio, including its alignment with the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and
  • quantity and value of a company’s IP (intellectual property) portfolio.

In addition, Statista researched various metrics around web traffic, to assess the relevance of the products and services to the respective target groups.

The evaluation process involved assessing all relevant companies within the global EdTech sector that exhibited above-average performance on financial metrics in their geographical region. Subsequently, the selection was narrowed down to include only those companies that not only excelled financially but also demonstrated significant industry impact within their specific categories. This selection process allowed us to establish our final ranking of the World's Top EdTech Companies 2026. Once the data was collected and evaluated, it was consolidated and weighted within a scoring model. The final score was calculated as follows: 70% x financial strength score + 30% x impact score. The companies with the highest score were awarded as "World's Top EdTech Companies 2026" by TIME and Statista.

Rising Stars

Alongside the list of 500 top EdTech companies, Statista and TIME are also publishing a “Rising Stars” ranking highlighting the companies with the highest revenue growth rates over the past three years out of those who submitted company data via the online application process. 

Applied criteria:

  • company age 10 years and younger
  • minimum revenue of 1 million US Dollars in 2024 
  • revenue growth rate of more than 20 % over the last three years

Disclaimer: The selection of the companies and the definition of the evaluation criteria were based on independent journalistic criteria of TIME and Statista. The evaluation was carried out by the statistics and market research company Statista. TIME and Statista make no claim to the completeness of the companies examined. The ranking only includes companies that qualify according to the criteria described in this document. A position in the ranking is a positive recognition based on research of publicly available data sources at the time and information received via an application process and through collaboration partners. In addition, events after June 4th, 2026, were not considered in the analysis. As such, the results of this list should not be used as the sole source of information for future deliberations. The information provided through this ranking should rather be considered in conjunction with other available information about a company. The quality of companies that are not included in the ranking is not disputed.

title: The World's Top EdTech Companies of 2026
summary:
Literacy rates have steadily risen around the world over the last decade, according to a 2025 UNESCO report—important progress on a key UN Sustainable Development Goal, as the ability to read, write, and use numbers is “crucial for thinking critically and navigating information-rich society and economy in a safe, effective and responsible manner.” Access to digital learning has largely been associated with higher test scores for students globally. As technology continues to advance, tech companies have pounced upon the opportunity to bring education systems around the world up to speed with the ever-more connected digital world and the proliferation of new tools like generative AI. 

To assess the top EdTech companies in the world, TIME partnered with Statista on a data-based research project evaluating the thousands of companies in the space on strong financial performance and industry impact. The end result is a list of the 500 top-performing companies in education technology.

Methodology: How TIME and Statista Determined the World's Top EdTech Companies of 2026

The top ranked company on the list is Duolingo, which was also the top-ranked EdTech company in the U.S. this year. The company, which started as a language learning app, has expanded into math, chess, and music. Duolingo now has over 60 million daily active users and generated more than $1 billion in bookings last year. As UNESCO advocates for more multilingualism, which can offer social, cognitive, and economic benefits, Duolingo’s chief product officer, Cem Kansu, believes that there are still more language learners the app has yet to reach. Roughly 20% of Duolingo’s users are in the U.S., with the majority distributed globally and Asia as one of their fastest growing regions recently. “Asia for English learning especially is a huge market,” Kansu says. Around half of Duolingo’s users are under 21, and use the app as an educational supplement—a lesser known product called Duolingo For Classrooms is designed specifically for teachers to assign Duolingo lessons as homework for students. 

Duolingo stands out among other language learning tools with engaging designs that motivate users to return and practice every day (more than 15 million users have a streak longer than one year); micro-lessons that use implicit learning rather than drilling grammar rules; and keeping its free tier to bring in new users.

“It is extremely important that we provide a very extensive free user experience because Duolingo was built around the idea of providing access to education,” says Kansu. “If someone that had to immigrate from Syria to Turkey had to learn Turkish to integrate, we want to provide access to them. On top of that, an excellent free product provides an amazing growth flywheel for Duolingo.” 

Word of mouth has certainly made Duolingo mainstream, but the company broke through the noise through its unconventional marketing tactics and its capitalization on cultural moments like the World Cup (daily learners studying Norwegian on Duolingo were up nearly 19% globally and 24% in the U.S. compared with the previous month), shows like Squid Game (Season 1 of Squid Game drove a 40% increase in new U.S. Korean learners on Duolingo immediately after its premiere), and Bad Bunny performing in the Super Bowl halftime show (engagement with Spanish jumped 35% the week after). 

While platforms like Duolingo are driving interest in learning and lowering the barrier for entry globally, in the U.S., where there appears to be a “learning recession” as standardized scores for math and reading drop, there are rising concerns about the use of technology in classrooms and too much screen time for children.

Emily Weinstein, a researcher at the Center for Digital Thriving at Harvard, says some students are using up to seven different apps to manage everything from grades to sports team schedules. Kids have reported feeling constantly tethered to these tools to monitor the “endless stream of notifications about what they're supposed to know and do,” which can add to the academic pressures they’re already experiencing, Weinstein says. Educators have also told her that these tools often arrive without the necessary onboarding. 

“Whenever you're thinking about technology in education, you should really think about it like a three-legged stool. You have the actual technology, you have the person using it, and then you have the place where they're using it,” says Stephen AguiIar, an associate professor at the USC Rossier School of Education. “In an ideal world, the technology works, the person knows how to use it, and it's used in the place where it's helpful or where it actually makes a difference. 

I think a lot of the backlash is about poor fit, where you have AI or EdTech companies entering a space they frankly know very little about, and then you have backlash from people who see things just not working. And what's a little unfortunate is that it doesn't always have anything to do with the core technology.”

A central problem is that educational institutions in the U.S. have been underfunded for decades, which creates strains in the system. “Whenever you put a system in strain, one of the things that happens is administrators rightly look for ways to cut costs and to become more efficient, even though education isn't an efficient enterprise,” says Aguilar. “Education is not this thing where you drop off your kids, they sit there for a little bit, knowledge gets poured into them, and then they come out a little smarter. That's the business way of looking at it, and it is fundamentally incorrect. Companies that do a little bit of a better job, they're really thinking about what teachers need to execute their work better.”

As some AI tools fuel the proliferation of digital cheating, there's a reckoning that's happening among educators about how they’re evaluating and assessing learning through traditional assignments, papers and homework, as well as how they’re teaching, experts say. Some leading EdTech platforms like Canvas-owner Instructure (no. 45) and Inspera (no. 31) have rolled out tools to deter AI cheating, including resources to help instructors understand the culture around cheating and how to change their focus from catching students cheating to creating an environment that encourages academic integrity. 

“The systemic issue is we don't have a sense of trust and integrity around the work, then we're trying to layer on EdTech as a solution, and kids are finding ways around it because they're missing the core thing that is going to give them pride in the work,” says Weinstein. “One of the things that we collectively need is to use this AI moment to have conversations in our classroom and school communities about what the purpose of learning is.”

From her research, Weinstein has found that listening more to student perspectives could fundamentally change how we understand what it looks and feels like to be a student in this context, and how these different technologies are shaping learning trajectories. “When you're talking to a young person, you can suddenly see that their good intentions are not always enough in a context where the market forces and design features are pulling them this way and that,” she says. “When I sit down with a kid and look at their ChatGPT logs, I can see such a difference in when they have turned to an EdTech tool for learning and when they have turned to it for a grade.”

Duolingo’s Kansu says that even though Duolingo For Schools’ dashboard for teachers had fairly good adoption, designing products for schools is not easy. “What we're realizing is if we just continue teaching better, Duolingo will become a great complement to classrooms anyway,” he says. “I'm hoping that Duolingo is always put in a bucket of good screen time…Meaning, any minute you spend on Duolingo, you are doing something good for yourself. Any fun minute you spend is also of extremely high learning value.”

title: The True Story Behind a DNA Test, a Family Reckoning, and My Grandfather Charles Manson
summary: At 22, Sophia Maddox learned that Charles Manson was her grandfather. So she made a documentary about reckoning with the shocking revelation.
full_text:
In 2022, Sophia Maddox received world-altering news in the middle of a casual phone call.
At the time, the 22-year-old aspiring actor and filmmaker was living in Los Angeles, working various jobs—mostly bussing tables and nannying—as she struggled to find auditions in the aftermath of the pandemic. She’d recently started a production company and directed a short film, but “it felt like my career was going nowhere,” Maddox tells TIME.
Then, after feeling sick on a flight home from New York City, she called her dad, Daniel Arguelles, and asked if he could drive her to get a
. As they were catching up on her trip, he suddenly dropped a bomb. “I think I found out who my dad is,” he told her. “It's really dark, and I don't think you're ready to know."
Arguelles had been raised by his mother and stepfather, and had never known his biological father. He’d been registered on
since 2015 with hopes of discovering the other piece of his parentage, but over the previous seven years he’d only matched with third cousins. “We kind of gave up on the idea that we'd find his dad,” Maddox says. Until he learned of a new match—to a user named Michael Brunner, who happened to share the same father: the notorious killer
Based on her dad’s language, Maddox immediately assumed it was someone famously violent. “I thought of Ted Bundy right away,” she says. “That was the darkest thing I could think of.” When Arguelles shared Manson’s name with her, once they were together in the car, Maddox didn’t quite recognize it. Her only point of reference was
Once Upon a Time…In Hollywood,
Quentin Tarantino's 2019 alternate history about the cult leader and the events leading to the infamous
1969 Tate-LaBianca murders
. Manson would be convicted on seven counts of first-degree murder; he
died in prison in 2017
after serving a life sentence.
Though this information would eventually inspire Maddox to make her first film, the new Hulu documentary
My Grandfather Charles Manson
, the news initially broke her. “It was very much like [the paternity scene] in
One Battle After Another
” Maddox says, referring to Chase Infiniti’s character in
Paul Thomas Anderson’s
film. “At the very end, he just put his arm around me as I sobbed while he was driving.” Later that night, she prayed that something had gone wrong with the DNA test, or that the website had made an error. But Brunner and Arguelles retook separate tests to confirm the source. Not long after, Arguelles subpoenaed Kern County, attained Manson’s DNA from his estate, and took another test that came back with a 99.9999 percent positive match. “My mental reality completely shifted,” Maddox says. “My existence changed because of this revelation.”
Thus began a cathartic, multi-year journey of self-discovery that Maddox chronicles in her documentary. Co-directed by Alexandra Orton, the film combines Maddox’s personal video diaries, therapy sessions, and exclusive interviews while descending into Manson’s early background and sensationalized media persona as a monster. “I’ve always been the good one,” Maddox cries in the film, reckoning with her contradicting bloodline.
“When Sophia told me the story, you just cannot believe it,” Orton says. “Everybody has to come to terms with skeletons in their family in some capacity, but it's never this extreme.”
From personal reckoning to making a film
Archival photos of Sophia and her father Daniel
The news didn’t immediately inspire Maddox to make a film. Instead, she spent a lot of time at home alone, lacking much support to process what she was going through. It wasn’t long before she turned to her phone. “I just started recording myself, not because I thought I was going to make a documentary. It was just cathartic,” she says. “You start processing it. You start talking to yourself like someone's in the room with you.”
But eventually, she felt like she had a story to tell. Eric Cook, her producing partner, gave her a camcorder to start filming more seriously. Over the next eight months, she recorded interviews—including one with her dad—created more self-tapes, pulled archival material, and compiled research to build a teaser video. “Once we made that sizzle reel together, we realized how helpful those video diaries were and how unfiltered and unproduced they really were,” Maddox says.
After a successful pitch to Hulu, Orton quickly joined the project to assist Maddox at the studio’s behest—a way for Hulu to maintain the film's objectivity and fill in any post-production gaps. Orton had previously worked on the genealogy show
Who Do You Think You Are?
and had experience with subjects dealing with unexpected news. “I was really used to counseling people and filming people as they learned surprising things about their family,” Orton says. “It was fascinating to watch this extremely brave, sharp young woman, who's also creative and expresses herself creatively, navigate everyone's fear on camera.”
The pair’s investigation starts at the Indiana boys reform school where Manson spent two years. Through records, Maddox learned her grandfather amassed 28 bad conduct reports, often the victim of (and sometimes the perpetrator of) physical punishment and sexual assault. In her quest for more insight into his personality, Maddox also contacted and interviewed former
members of his cult family
Lynette “Squeaky” Fromme
, Dianne Lake, and Stephanie Schram—along with some figures from Manson’s more recent past, including a man who calls himself Blackwolf, who recorded around 800 calls with Manson before he died.
Maddox supplements their interviews with expert insights (Stephen Kay, the last living prosecutor during the Manson trial, makes an appearance), old news footage, and the conventional “Helter Skelter” theories that have populated Manson’s mythos, showcasing the contradictions in how the notorious killer was perceived. As she explains, her ambition was to “look at all sides."
“I think what makes this film different from any
other Manson documentary
, besides my personal connection, is that a lot of people don’t bother to look at people on the fringes of society who have a different background and lifestyle,” Maddox says. “I'm not taking their stories as fact. It's just a collection of data. That was always my intention.”
“There were definitely some nerves about sending a young woman into these scenarios,” Orton admits, noting that Maddox was always surrounded by a camera crew. “We had a lot of background conversations to make sure we felt adequately prepared and understood where we were going.”
Perhaps the biggest insight came from Maddox’s attempts to speak with law enforcement and contemporary historians of Manson. The filmmakers found that even mentioning her bloodline repelled potential subjects from agreeing to be interviewed. “They would hear ‘granddaughter’ and immediately make a judgment about her that had nothing to do with who she is,’” Orton says. “She's an amazing, trustworthy, kind human being who has nothing to do with her grandfather.”
The impact on a father-daughter bond
An archival image of Manson in My Grandfather Charles Manson
The relationship between Maddox and her father provides the documentary’s most complicated and emotionally compelling throughline. As a kid in Southern California, Maddox lived in separate homes with her divorced parents, with Arguelles cultivating her love for the arts. But as she grew older, she became more curious about her father’s upbringing, often asking her grandmother, Darlene, about who her dad’s biological father was.
As Maddox explains in the documentary, Darlene, who died in 2020, had a brief romantic encounter with “Charlie Dear,” whom she met at a bus stop when she was 17 years old. Ten years after Arguelles was born in 1959, Darlene realized Manson was likely the father when his name began popping up in headlines. The resemblance is striking. “Manson’s picture popped up, and that's when I went, ‘OK, yeah, that's your dad,’” Maddox remembers.

title: How to Support Someone Without Giving Advice
summary: Stop trying to fix it. Start helping instead.
full_text:
When someone you care about is going through a hard time, you'd probably do anything to help them
. Yet one of the easiest traps to fall into is offering advice too soon.
"We'll often jump into, 'How can I fix this? How can I
?'" says Alli Spotts-De Lazzer, a therapist in Chattanooga, Tenn. “But advice usually lands better after someone
." Otherwise, rushing to offer solutions can leave people feeling dismissed instead of supported. Experts say the best way to show up is to help people feel heard first and offer guidance later, if they want it.
Here's exactly how to support someone you love—without leading with advice.
Ask yourself who you’re really trying to soothe
Before you say anything, run a quick gut check: "Is what I'm about to say going to help me, or help them?" You might be surprised by your answer. "Giving advice usually calms you down more than it helps them," says Cheryl Groskopf, a marriage and family therapist and professional clinical counselor in Los Angeles. Watching someone you love struggle creates uncertainty in you, too—which is exactly why the urge to jump in and fix things can be so hard to resist.
The reality is, you probably can't solve what they're facing. You can't tell them whether they'll get the job, whether the relationship will work out, or how a difficult decision will unfold. Instead of trying to erase that uncertainty, help them tolerate it. Groskopf suggests offering comfort like this: "You might not need to have all the answers right now." "Supporting someone means helping them discover that they can survive not knowing yet,” she says.
Help them feel less alone
Before advice can land, people need to feel like you actually get them. Spotts-De Lazzer likens it to sitting quietly beside someone on a bench instead of trying to solve their problem. The most helpful responses are often short—and don't start with "I": "That sounds hard." "That's a lot." "That sucks." Said sincerely, they let someone know they don't have to carry what they're feeling alone.
You don't need to fix their problem—you just need to stay with them long enough for them to feel understood. One line Spotts-De Lazzer especially likes: "Can I sit with you in this for a minute, just so you're not alone?"
Let them stay the expert on their own life
The goal isn't to know more than the person in front of you—it's to make it clear that you see them. That starts with empathy, but many of us aren't sure what that actually sounds like. Try "It makes sense you feel that way" or "I can understand why you'd feel that way," suggests Mary McLaughlin, a licensed clinical social worker in Vienna, Va. Then get curious and let them lead: "Position yourself so that they're the expert," she says. "Let them be the expert on what they're sharing."
The fastest way to make someone feel misunderstood is to act like you know their situation better than they do. McLaughlin recalls a client whose wife had
; what stung most, he told her, was people who rushed to share what some expert or relative had done. "It's just so deflating," she says. "Like, don't you think I've already thought of these things?" When you do want to nudge someone toward a decision, ask instead of instruct: "What comes to mind when you think about doing this?" That's powerful because, as McLaughlin puts it, "they hear their own voice in the answer."
Don't guess what they need
Not everyone wants the same kind of support. Instead of assuming you know what would help, ask. "Start a conversation with, 'I'm so here for you. What do you need?'" says Melissa Gluck, a psychologist in New York. "Do you want me to be in fix-it mode? Do you want me to just sit and listen?" It takes only a few seconds to ask, and it can spare you one of the most common missteps: solving a problem the other person never asked you to.
Some people won't know what they need, and that's fine—you can read their cues as you go. But many people know exactly what they're after, whether it's reassurance or simply the sense that they're not overreacting. "I know we're all so afraid to ask," Gluck says, "but we don't have to be."
Sometimes the most supportive thing you can do is...nothing. At least for a second. "That one beat—just taking a second—will often give that person much more safety and regulation than any amount of words," Groskopf says. Rushing in with "Have you tried...?" can push someone toward solutions before they've had a chance to process what they're feeling.
There's a physiological reason a calm presence helps: "
sync with other nervous systems—that's what co-regulation is," Groskopf says. That’s also why big, alarmed reactions can backfire. Reacting with "Oh my God, that's such a big deal" can unintentionally make someone feel like their emotions are something to fear. Steadiness sends the opposite message: "Your emotions make sense, and they're survivable."
Trade fixes for curiosity
If you're tempted to tell someone what you think they should do, ask a question instead. Gluck likes this one: "It sounds like part of you already knows what you'd do—what's stopping you?" Instead of handing someone an answer, it invites them to think through what's really holding them back.
It also does something practical: It gets people unstuck. "Usually when you're
, you're stuck in your head," she says. A good question can help someone move forward, without you having to solve the problem for them.
Before you jump in to solve someone else's problem, McLaughlin suggests pausing and asking yourself one blunt question: "Whose problem is this?" Even with the best intentions, stepping in can make someone feel like you don't trust them to figure things out. "When you're solving, you're basically saying, 'I don't really believe you can handle this, so I'm going to handle it for you,'" she says.
Instead, remind them of what they're capable of. Try saying, "I've seen you work through hard things before." Sometimes, McLaughlin says, "you have to have confidence in someone until they can find it in themselves."
Skip the silver lining
When someone is hurting, it's natural to reach for reassurance. But if you offer it too soon, it can land as dismissive instead of comforting. "Cheer up" and "It's going to be fine" can fall flat because, as Spotts-De Lazzer points out, you don't have a crystal ball. Comparisons like "Others have it worse" tend to miss the mark too, minimizing a person's experience instead of acknowledging it. "The person owns their experience in that moment," she says. "It's their subjective truth, their emotional truth."
That doesn't mean you can't offer hope—it's just a matter of timing. Acknowledge the pain first, then offer reassurance: "I know it'll pass. But right now it sucks, and I'm here." People are much more likely to believe your encouragement after they feel like you've understood what they're going through.
Show up with your hands, not just your words
Support isn't just something you say—it can also be something you do. Drop off dinner, send a gift card, or offer to grab their kid from school, especially when someone's slogging through a hard stretch. Small, practical gestures can take one thing off a person's plate at a time when even everyday tasks feel overwhelming. Better yet, don't wait to be asked. "Most of us don't want to ask for that," Gluck says, "so when you don't have to, it means a lot."
And if you're genuinely unsure what would help, don't let that stop you from reaching out. "I'd rather get it wrong, but I want to do something," Spotts-De Lazzer says. After all, the goal isn't to say the perfect thing or respond perfectly every time. As she puts it, "It's not about getting anything right. It's about demonstrating care."

title: The Allies Who Cannot Afford to Quit America
summary: For America's Asian allies, support from Washington remains the most effective deterrent against Chinese hegemony.
full_text:
These are not easy days for America’s allies. From Europe to the Middle East to the Asia-Pacific, security partners of the United States are treading carefully, fearful of antagonizing President Donald Trump, who has cast Washington’s closest allies as freeloaders, slapped them with steep tariffs, and even questioned the sovereignty of some allies with outlandish claims.
Nowhere are the stakes higher than in the Asia-Pacific. The region
more stable compared to Europe or the Middle East, but it is anything but placid: a rising China is pressing for greater influence in a region where American primacy—and that of its allies—once went largely unchallenged.
As if to underscore this point, China chose July 6—the day before the NATO summit began in Ankara—to test and fire a
long-range ballistic missile
from a nuclear submarine, which landed in the
South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone
. The launch of a missile capable of reaching the continental U.S. drew attention to China’s massive
and its growing capacity to threaten American cities should Washington come to the aid of regional allies in a conflict with Beijing. The missile test may be a demonstration of China’s new capability, but it is also a reminder of a longstanding threat.
Washington and several U.S. allies in the Asia-Pacific criticized the “irresponsible” test. Still, the episode reinforced allies’ longstanding concerns about the effectiveness and reliability of the U.S. security guarantees to deter an ever more powerful China. What are American allies and partners supposed to do about it? The answers vary across the region
but every answer points toward a stronger American role.
Unease in the Asia-Pacific
There is no equivalent of NATO in Asia. The security arrangements in the region have been based primarily on the hub and spoke system that Washington created after World War II, when it signed alliance treaties with the Philippines, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, and Thailand. The U.S. also signed a mutual defense treaty with Taiwan in 1954, but terminated it in 1980 after normalization with China in 1979. However, these American allies—the spokes—did not necessarily have defense obligations to each other. All of these countries, to varying degrees, rely on U.S. assurances to deter China from using its military muscle to impose its will on them and the broader region.
Nearly every Asian capital has by now grown less certain that Washington will honor those commitments if put to the test. And while Trump does not tend to rant against Asian allies as he does against NATO partners, this offers little comfort to Asian capitals. at a test range in April, while Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan are setting up new production lines for missiles of their own.
This strategy of arming up while working hard to keep the U.S. close is not new. A series of reports by the International Crisis Group on
military modernization across the region
traces how some of Washington’s Asian allies and partners have been following a similar playbook for several years now. Only now, they have stronger incentives.

The rearmament effort predates Trump’s second term, but pressure from Washington has only added momentum. Tokyo’s purchase of Tomahawk missiles from the U.S., along with the new indigenous long-range munitions it is producing, would still

Japan is also stepping up its diplomacy with other regional players, as necessary in a period of American retrenchment and amid growing

South Korea has vowed to increase its defense spending from 2.3% of its GDP to as much as 3.6% and has earned praise from Washington as a “

Seoul is also considering its options for confronting
North Korea’s nuclear advancement

title: Building AI infrastructure with the Effingham County community
summary: OpenAI announces Project Camellia in Effingham County, Georgia, with commitments to responsible energy, community investment, jobs, and access to Codex.
full_text:
Building AI infrastructure with the Effingham County community
Project Camellia is a long-term datacenter project that OpenAI is designing and developing in Effingham County, Georgia. To support the data center, we are contracting with Georgia Power Company for 3.2 gigawatts of power which will be delivered in phases between 2028 and 2032.
We’re excited about the opportunity to work with this community. We also recognize that new data center projects can raise important questions, so we’ve outlined our initial commitments that will guide how we engage, develop, and operate.
1. Electricity rates will not go up for residents because of this project. Georgia families will not subsidize this project. OpenAI will pay the full cost of the infrastructure and electric-service costs required to serve it. Under Georgia Public Service Commission rules, those costs cannot be passed on to existing ratepayers. Also, this project will be one of the first data centers designed to proactively reduce its power consumption before residential customers are impacted during periods of high demand, so we can meaningfully support the reliability of Georgia Power’s electric system and support our neighbors.
2. Water use is minimal. The project will use a closed-loop water system, which recirculates water rather than continuously withdrawing and discharging. It works like a car radiator and is intended to keep ongoing water use low. The water used will not divert water from local communities and the ongoing water needs will be for people to use in an ordinary workplace setting such as restrooms, kitchens, sanitation, and maintenance and will be similar to an office building with the same amount of employees.
3. We are committed to making sure local communities benefit. OpenAI will provide $80 million in community benefits over the life of the project, informed by the community and directed toward local priorities such as schools, public safety, health care, utilities, workforce training, housing, veterans’ services, and support for small businesses and working families. This commitment is separate from projected tax revenue and the Codex credits described below. We will pay hundreds of millions of dollars in state and local tax revenue and expect to be the largest taxpayer in the county. The project will create thousands of construction and permanent on-site jobs and prioritize local contractors and businesses.
In addition to the $80 million in community benefits, we will make up to $71 million in credits for Codex available to eligible Georgia college, community college, and technical school students. Codex is OpenAI’s agentic coding tool, now available within ChatGPT, that helps people build software and complete technical projects. Eligible students will receive $100 in credits through their ChatGPT accounts to extend their use of Codex, gain hands-on experience with agentic AI, build projects, and develop practical skills for careers across engineering, manufacturing, health care, education, entrepreneurship, and the skilled trades. Georgia students will be able to access their free Codex credits at chatgpt.com/codex/georgia-college-students/(opens in a new window)
4. Being accountable. To help ensure the project meets these commitments, an annual publicly available audit by an independent firm will be conducted and released.
We have been meeting with state and local officials, community leaders, schools, and other regional partners to learn about local priorities and gather feedback on the project. On Thursday, July 23, we will hold a public open house where residents can meet the project team, ask questions, and help shape how the project delivers for Effingham County. Input from the open house and continued conversations with residents, local officials, schools, businesses, and community organizations will help shape a Georgia Community Compact to memorialize these commitments. The Compact will translate community priorities into specific commitments and clear accountability measures as the project develops.
We believe showing up early is the right way to build trust, with that, we are still at the beginning of the development process. Significant work remains on infrastructure, project phasing, design, financing, and operating model. As we work through these details, we intend to engage with local communities, government, workforce organizations, and our infrastructure and financing partners.
The proposed site is located within the Savannah Gateway Industrial Hub, a pre-existing industrially-zoned warehouse project. This project is expected to generate materially less traffic than a warehouse project on the same site, while also using less water, creating stronger long-term tax revenue, and supporting more durable on-site employment.
AI can help accelerate science and medicine, expand access to better tools for learning and discovery, create new kinds of jobs and businesses, and make everyday work more productive. Computing infrastructure is one of the main factors determining how quickly AI can improve, how reliably it works, and how broadly it can be used.
Building this infrastructure in the United States strengthens domestic industry, creates good jobs, and helps ensure American communities participate in the economic opportunity created by AI. Project Camellia can help build that foundation while creating lasting opportunity in Effingham County and Southeast Georgia, and would be entirely privately funded.
We are already seeing that potential take shape in Abilene, Texas(opens in a new window), where our first campus is operating at scale, training frontier models, and supporting thousands of jobs.
There is significant work ahead, and we will share more information as the plans develop. For the latest information on the project, please visit www.projectcamellia.com(opens in a new window).

title: Introducing OpenAI Presence
summary: Introducing OpenAI Presence, a proven enterprise AI agent platform that helps organizations deploy trusted voice and chat agents for customer and internal workflows.
full_text:
The challenge for enterprises is no longer proving that AI agents can work, it’s making them reliable enough to do high-value work in production. Agent behavior must also adapt as products, policies, and user behavior change. That requires more than a model: it requires the systems, evaluations, and deployment expertise to improve agents as those conditions change without giving up control.
We’re introducing OpenAI Presence, a battle-tested product that helps enterprises deploy trusted AI agents that can answer questions, resolve issues, use company systems, take approved actions, and escalate to people when needed. Proven through years of working with customers at enterprise-scale, Presence pairs model reasoning with policies, guardrails, and escalation rules that verify accuracy and performance.
Each deployment starts with a specific job, such as resolving billing issues, supporting insurance claims, or resolving employee IT service requests. The agent receives only the knowledge and system access required for that job. The company sets the policies: what the agent can do, when it needs approval, and when a person should take over. After launch, production sessions and escalations reveal gaps. Codex proposes updates that teams can test and approve, helping the agent adapt as customer behavior changes.
OpenAI works alongside each customer to identify each high-value workflow, connect the necessary knowledge and systems, establish permissions and policies, test the agent, and bring it into production. As the deployment expands, OpenAI and select systems integrators can continue to support it. Presence was developed in tight collaboration with OpenAI’s Research team, with generalized insights from every deployment informing ongoing research and product development and improving the product for all customers over time.
Today, Presence supports real-time experiences across voice and chat, such as customer support, outbound sales, and high-risk internal workflows. A customer might use it to resolve a billing issue—from understanding the request and verifying the customer to looking up account information, applying company policy, and taking an approved action.
Companies decide what remains consistent across deployments—such as policies, evaluations, and escalation rules—and what should change for each workflow or channel. This lets teams build on what works and expand to new use cases without starting over.
Presence brings together the components teams need to run agents in production: policies and standard operating procedures, guardrails, approved actions, simulations, evaluation tools, and a Codex-powered improvement process.
Together, these components help teams connect company systems, define how agents should behave, evaluate performance, enforce policies, and manage changes after launch.
Built through years of deploying agents with customers, Presence is an ambitious product shaped by the demands of mission-critical environments. Every deployment generated insights that continuously inform OpenAI research and product development, creating compounding benefits for customers.
Presence powers OpenAI’s English-language phone support channel at 1-888-GPT‑0090, handling open-ended requests, verifying callers, using account context, and taking approved actions. Within weeks, it met or exceeded benchmarks we use to grade frontline human-support quality and now resolves 75% of inbound issues without human assistance. Working with our launch team, its Codex-powered improvement loop reduced human handoffs by 15 percentage points in just 10 days.
Leading enterprises are also building on the same proven foundation:
- BBVA is exploring AI-powered voice support for everyday banking needs in Mexico.
- SoftBank is testing natural Japanese-language customer conversations.
- IAG is exploring timely support during high-demand events such as severe weather.
Before a Presence deployment reaches users, teams can test it against common requests, edge cases, and higher-risk scenarios. Simulations and graders check whether it reached the right outcome, followed policy, used tools correctly, and escalated when appropriate. Guardrails can intervene when an interaction moves outside the company’s boundaries.
That work does not stop at launch. Production sessions, escalations, and quality signals can show teams where an agent is working well and where it needs attention as policies, products, and user behavior change. Codex using the Presence plugin investigates those signals and suggests updates. Teams can test each proposed change against the version in production, then approve a controlled rollout.
Presence is also designed to learn with you—improving as your business, customers, and employees evolve while the business stays in control. Built on OpenAI’s world-class research, it continues to advance as our models and capabilities improve. When a use case goes beyond what the product supports today, OpenAI Forward Deployed Engineers (FDEs) and partners can work with the customer to bring it into production.
OpenAI Presence is available to eligible enterprise customers as a deployed product through a limited general availability program. Deployments are led by OpenAI Forward Deployed Engineers and select global systems integrators. Presence is not yet available as a self-serve product.
As we introduce OpenAI Presence, we'll continue supporting voice customers with access to our frontier models through the OpenAI API.
To explore whether Presence is right for your organization, contact your OpenAI account team.

summary: Gentle Monster glasses, Warby Parker glasses, a prompt asking for the history behind a pictured building, and a prompt asking to book a table at a pictured restaurant
full_text:
3 Google updates from Galaxy Unpacked 2026
Today at Galaxy Unpacked in London, we celebrated the launch of the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, Fold8, and Flip8. With these devices, we are making it easier than ever to get started on Android while also rolling out the first capabilities of Gemini Intelligence 1 — our vision for technology that works proactively for you. Whether you choose to unfold your phone to maximize your productivity on a bigger screen or keep it folded so you can focus on your day, Gemini Intelligence is there to help with the heavy lifting.
Here is a look at three updates coming to the newest devices.
1. Get next-generation task automation with Gemini Intelligence.
Gemini Intelligence can help you offload digital chores so you can spend less time behind a screen. Back in February, we introduced a beta for task automation, helping you delegate simple everyday tasks to Gemini, such as ordering a rideshare or getting your favorite takeout meal for delivery.
Now task automation is expanding support from a handful of apps to more than 40 popular apps. 2 This means Gemini can now help you handle more of your daily "life admin" — from shopping and making dinner reservations to booking travel experiences and buying event tickets. On the Galaxy Z Flip8, you can even access this assistance directly from the Flex Window by long pressing the power button.
Plus, Gemini can now use advanced reasoning to understand what is on your screen and parse complex images as prompts. This gives you a powerful jumpstart — because sometimes, the easiest way to explain what you need is to show Gemini a shopping list or inspiration photo.
While Gemini works to complete the task, you can track the step-by-step progress on your screen, multitask in other apps, or close your phone and let Gemini run in the background. If you need to make a quick adjustment or add a personal touch, you can step in to handle a specific detail and then hand control back to Gemini to complete the rest. Gemini is designed to notify you when the task is ready for your review and final confirmation.
2. Raise the bar on your projects with Gemini Notebook.
To help you manage deep projects and synthesize complex information, we are bringing the power of Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM) directly to your device. The app comes preinstalled on Samsung's new foldables. 3
Gemini Notebook is your thinking and research partner powered by our advanced multimodal models. On the Galaxy Z Fold8 series' expansive display, you can drag and drop photos, documents, whiteboard images, voice recordings, and more directly into a side-by-side workspace.
You can use the chat function in Gemini Notebook to ask questions about your sources or go one step further and create custom, high-quality resources — including slide decks, videos, flash cards, quizzes, or even a podcast — tailored to how you learn best.
To help you tackle your most ambitious projects, we are including a six-month trial of Google AI Pro on every Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, Fold8, and Flip8, which gives you more access to powerful features, such as Audio Overviews, Video Overviews, Slides, and more.
3. Take Gemini on the go with watches and glasses.
Our collaboration with Samsung extends beyond smartphones. On the Galaxy Watch 9, you have more convenient access to Gemini on the go. Simply raise your wrist and Gemini will activate so you can ask it questions, no wake word required.
We’re also bringing Gemini to glasses. At Google I/O 2026, we announced intelligent eyewear — created in partnership with Samsung and launching this fall — and shared two designs from our partners, eyewear brands Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. Today we revealed two more frames and shared more about how Gemini’s helpfulness will come to life on these new devices. For example if you’re wearing a compatible Wear OS watch, you’ll be able to control your glasses with just a hand gesture.
Whether you are looking to simplify your daily routine or boost your productivity, today's announcements are just the beginning of what we have in store. We will roll out more intelligent features as they are ready, so you’re not left waiting.

title: Samsung’s newest foldable finally feels Ultra
summary: While we wait for Apple's rumored foldable iPhone, Samsung is polishing a design it already has on the market. I just spent three hours with my hands on the new Z Fold 8 Ultra, and all I can think about is how Samsung finally made the crease invisible. Samsung says it achieved this thanks to […]
full_text:
While we wait for Apple’s rumored foldable iPhone, Samsung is polishing a design it already has on the market. I just spent three hours with my hands on the new Z Fold 8 Ultra, and all I can think about is how Samsung finally made the crease invisible.
Samsung’s newest foldable finally feels Ultra
One small step for phones, one giant leap for foldables.
Samsung says it achieved this thanks to its new Flex Titanium display tech. Its foldable screens now utilize a titanium film that sits below the OLED panel, which Samsung says has 20-times the mechanical stiffness as opposed to the polymer film it used in its old foldables. This film is bonded to a new titanium plate, and when used together, the crease that used to plague foldable devices is practically nonexistent. I spent a lot of time pressing my finger down on the center of the screen trying to feel the crease. If you apply a lot of force and are specifically looking for it, you can feel it ever so slightly, but I came away very impressed with how minor it is. In day-to-day use, there’s very little chance you’re going to notice it.
Oppo recently did away with its crease, too, albeit in a different way. It used 3D liquid printing to fill the uneven gaps in the Find N6 hinge. I haven’t had the opportunity to use that device, but if it’s as impressive as Samsung’s technology, we may be well into the no-crease foldable future.
The new Fold 8 Ultra mimics the silhouette of last year’s Fold7 almost to a tee, but it has improved on just about everything that made the Fold7 great. Core specs of the Fold 8 include the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy, 256GB of base storage, and 12GB of RAM, which are all identical to the S26 Ultra. And the battery has been improved, too, bumping the phone to a 5,000mAh cell also in line with the S26 Ultra. This is a fairly significant upgrade from the 4,400mAh battery we saw on the Fold7, and it’s mostly due to a chemistry change. Samsung confirmed that it’s finally using silicon carbon technology in the Fold 8 Ultra.
That chemistry change also came with a charging upgrade. The Fold 8 Ultra can now charge at 45W on a wired connection and 20W on a wireless charger, up from 25W wired and 15W wireless in last year’s Fold. Samsung says the phone itself doesn’t have magnets included in order to keep it as thin as possible, so while it’s not a Qi2 device technically, it will be “Qi2 ready” with compatible magnet-equipped cases.
The cameras are also a bit more in line with the S26 Ultra. The main and telephoto cameras are the same 200mp and 10mp sensors as last year’s Z Fold7, but the ultrawide has been updated to 50mp to match the S26 Ultra. This enables dual 8k video recording out of the main and ultrawide sensors on the phone. You still aren’t getting the fourth 10x telephoto lens yet, though. Maybe we’ll see it next year. There are some software updates to the camera this year, too. The Fold 8 Ultra now supports the APV pro video codec introduced in the S26 series, and you can edit the footage directly inside Samsung’s gallery app with built-in color styles.
Samsung also has some updates to it and Google’s AI features, optimized for foldable displays. Samsung’s “Now Nudge” proactive notification feature that suggests actions based on what’s on your screen has been optimized for the Fold 8 Ultra’s display. Now Nudge will now show up as a floating bubble on the side of the screen as well as in your notification shade when it identifies an action you can take. For example, if someone texts you asking what your calendar looks like next week, the feature will now show up as an ambient floating bubble, as well as a notification in your notification tray. If you tap it, it will open your email app in a split-screen view.
Google’s Gemini’s Automated Tasks feature is now optimized for foldables, too. Now when you ask Gemini to complete a task for you with the screen unfolded, the phone will create a pop-up window with the task in progress so it doesn’t take up your entire screen. You can also have it work in the background minimized, but it’s nice to be able to work on other things while still keeping an eye on how Gemini is running through your task. Screen context is making its way to the Fold 8 Ultra as well, allowing you to do things like add events on your screen directly to your calendar.
And finally, Samsung is introducing a new “Fan Cam” feature across its foldable lineup, which can take footage recorded on the phone, identify subjects, and cut the video into various horizontal and vertical aspect ratios. This is useful for creators who need to deliver footage in different formats for clients. In practice, the edits feel a bit “floaty,” with the finished product giving a sense that it’s moving around ever so slightly, even if the source footage is incredibly stable. What is stable is Samsung’s Super Steady Horizontal Lock feature, which debuted on the S26 series, and is coming to all its new devices it debuted today.
All of these upgrades aren’t without price bumps, though. The Fold 8 Ultra will start at $2,099.99 for the base 256GB/12GB model. This is a $100 increase over last year’s Fold7 of the same storage and RAM SKU. With the price of everything becoming more expensive by the month, this isn’t exactly surprising, but that doesn’t make the fact that paying over two thousand dollars for a phone is going to be a massive investment for just about anyone — especially one that starts at 256GB.

title: Samsung’s wider Z Fold 8 feels just right
summary: A year after overhauling its Z Fold phone with a radically thinner design, Samsung has changed things up again, this time altering the shape entirely. The Z Fold 8 is wider than any of Samsung's previous foldables, and shorter too, a size and shape somewhere between Samsung's traditional Flip and Fold models. In photos, I […]
full_text:
A year after overhauling its Z Fold phone with a radically thinner design, Samsung has changed things up again, this time altering the shape entirely. The Z Fold 8 is wider than any of Samsung’s previous foldables, and shorter too, a size and shape somewhere between Samsung’s traditional Flip and Fold models.
Samsung’s wider Z Fold 8 feels just right
But $1,900 is a hell of a lot for a phone with no telephoto camera.
In photos, I wasn’t impressed by the squat shape. In person, to my surprise, it feels great, and almost immediately intuitive. If you want to get a feel for it yourself, grab your passport — the Z Fold 8 is about the same height and less than half an inch thinner.
This isn’t Samsung’s only new foldable this year, and in fact, its lineup just got more confusing. The Z Fold 8 may be the official follow-up to last year’s impressive Z Fold 7, but in truth the Z Fold 8 Ultra is the straightforward sequel. That phone has the same squarish inner screen as previous Z Fold phones and a similar triple rear camera. The name feels like a sly trick to get around this year’s inevitable price hikes: Samsung slapped “Ultra” on the box of its highest-end model to help cover for pricing the phone at $2,099.99, up $100 from the Z Fold 7.
Meanwhile, with its wider screens and stripped back cameras, the Z Fold 8 feels less like a sequel and more like a spinoff. And it almost — almost — looks like a bargain at $1,899.99, down $100 on its nominal predecessor.
Samsung isn’t the first to the Z Fold 8’s form factor. Huawei’s Pura X Max launched in April with a similar shape, though it’s only available in China. Apple is widely expected to be next, using a similar passport-esque shape for its first iPhone foldable in September. In truth, elements of this design are even older: The Fold 8 is almost exactly the same width as Google’s first-gen Pixel Fold, though a good deal shorter, bringing foldable phones full circle.
I’ve been skeptical about the return of the wider foldable, which in photos looks squat and uncomfortable, too wide to use naturally while closed and too short to feel expansive when open. The industry tried this design once and moved on, so why — other than Apple’s potential adoption — should we give it a go again?
Samsung’s answer is that its two Z Fold 8 models are designed for different users and different uses. The Z Fold 8 Ultra, tall and thin when closed and similar to a square when open, is meant to be a multitasking monster, useful for running apps in split-screen, giving you the equivalent screen space of two regular 6.5-inch phones side by side. The wider Z Fold 8 is instead about consumption: Its 4:3 aspect ratio is equally natural for watching Netflix shows in landscape as it is for reading ebooks in portrait, and at 201g, it’s light enough to hold comfortably in one hand.
Or, as Samsung’s marketing department puts it, the Fold 8 is for “joy-maxxing,” and the Ultra is for “power-maxxing.” I sit through these presentations so that you don’t have to, folks.
The 4:3 display isn’t widescreen, so you’ll still get letterboxing at the top and bottom when watching most videos, whether on YouTube or a streaming service. But unlike Samsung’s previous squarish Folds, which weren’t much wider than simply turning your phone on its side, opening the Z Fold 8 up really does fit more video onto your screen, and the wider aspect ratio will be much more natural for gaming too. It feels less like a foldable and more like a tablet and is all the better for it.
I’m still a little uncertain whether I like how the Z Fold 8 feels closed — the way I use foldables the majority of the time. The width of the 10:16 cover display is less noticeable than I expected, and I got used to using the phone this way remarkably quickly, but I’m worried it might feel less comfortable if you stick the phone in a case. The reduced height proves an unexpected blessing here, making it easier and more comfortable to stretch across the screen one-handed than on larger slab phones like the S26 Ultra. A lot will depend on how well apps adapt to the shorter screen, though Samsung has already announced that Instagram is on board with optimizations.
There are other considerations to the Fold 8 than its new shape. The Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset, optimized together with Samsung, makes this about as powerful as any other flagship out there. The 120Hz OLED main display is the same in specs as the Fold 8 Ultra’s, including an impressive peak brightness of 3,000 nits and a new anti-reflective coating to reduce glare. It supports the same new software features as the Z Fold 8 Ultra, including the official launch of Gemini Intelligence task automation and a proactive AI feature called Now Nudge that pops up with cross-app suggestions to add an event to your calendar or send someone an email.
For the first time, Samsung has caught up with its Chinese competition and adopted silicon-carbon batteries, a new type of lithium ion cell that incorporates a small amount of silicon alongside the graphite in the anode. Silicon-carbon batteries can squeeze higher capacities into smaller spaces, but they come with a downside: The highly reactive silicon is less stable, and there are fears that silicon-carbon batteries will lose capacity more quickly over time.
The 4,800mAh battery capacity of the Fold 8 isn’t an enormous jump from the 4,400mAh in the Fold 7 and pales in comparison to the biggest foldable battery around, Honor’s 6,660mAh Magic V6. A cautious approach to silicon-carbon is understandable from Samsung, which still bears the scars of the disastrous Galaxy Note 7 battery, which prompted a full recall of that phone in 2016 over safety concerns.
“Silicon-carbon cells must be carefully managed,” BD Yang, executive vice president of Samsung’s core component technology team, told The Verge, emphasizing Samsung’s work to manage silicon reactivity, swelling, and long-term cell stability, rather than prioritizing energy density alone. He called the Fold 8’s battery an “end-to-end improvement” over previous generations, combining higher capacity with “dependable performance.”
Less encouraging are the cameras. Unlike Samsung’s previous Fold models, the Fold 8 is limited to two rear cameras, with no telephoto to be found. Both the main and ultrawide lenses use 50-megapixel sensors, which looks like an upgrade for the ultrawide, but means the main lens might be worse than the Z Fold 7’s 200-megapixel shooter — though we won’t know for sure until Samsung shares detailed specs like the sensor size and aperture and I get the chance to put the cameras to a more thorough test in my review. Still, Samsung’s foldable cameras already lagged behind its best slab phones, and the Fold 8 only appears to make matters worse.
It’s also fallen behind the foldable competition in a few key ways. All three of Samsung’s new foldables remain limited to IP48, meaning they lack the comprehensive dust protection of Google’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold. And while Samsung says it’s overhauled the hinge and display stack with a new titanium-alloy film and a titanium plate below it, the changes aren’t enough to make the display crease anywhere near as subtle as on Oppo’s Find N6. Better are new magnets, which make the phone easier to open one-handed, and help it close with a satisfying click — though Samsung is still stubbornly refusing to integrate the internal magnets required for full Qi2 charging support.
I won’t really know whether the Fold 8’s form factor is for me until I’ve spent more time with the phone, but after an hour or so, I’m surprisingly sold. I’ve never figured out a way to replace my work laptop with a foldable phone, but I could easily see one supplanting my tablet, which has been mostly relegated to a portable screen for in-flight entertainment. And with a bigger battery to boot, the Z Fold 8 might just last ’til I land.
Still: $1,900 is an awful lot for any phone, and especially one that’s suffered such an ob

title: Samsung’s Galaxy Watch 9 and Ultra 2 bet big on battery
summary: It's a year of refinement for the Galaxy Watch. With the new Galaxy Watch 9 and Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, which are being announced today, Samsung is more or less taking what people like about its watches and tweaking those elements to be better. The company has been doing this for the past few generations […]
full_text:
It’s a year of refinement for the Galaxy Watch. With the new Galaxy Watch 9 and Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, which are being announced today, Samsung is more or less taking what people like about its watches and tweaking those elements to be better. The company has been doing this for the past few generations of its watch line, but this year’s updates seem focused on shoring up Samsung’s wearable weaknesses. Namely, battery life and preventive health features.
Samsung’s Galaxy Watch 9 and Ultra 2 bet big on battery
The watches sport a new chip, bigger batteries, and new health metrics. But the updates come with another price hike.
The Ultra 2, now $50 more expensive at $699.99, gets a few key spec bumps. The 47mm watch packs in a whopping 800mAh battery — a major 35 percent increase from the 590mAh battery in the original Ultra. I got around 70 hours on the original Ultra, so I’m curious to see how this battery boost translates to everyday usage. I was worried the larger battery would necessitate a chonkier watch, but surprisingly, the case is 12 percent thinner, measuring 10.7mm. The standard strap is also about 1mm thinner at 1.9mm, and a bit softer to the touch.
Another tweak for outdoors enthusiasts: The watch now has a 5,000-nit display with thinner bezels around the sides. That level of brightness might seem excessive, but it’s meant to improve visibility in direct sunlight. I wasn’t invited to see the watches in person, but my colleague Owen Grove saw the watch indoors and said the display looked slightly brighter than the Watch 9, which has a 3,000-nit display. That gives the Ultra 2 the brightest smartwatch screen and among the biggest batteries.
The Ultra 2 is also getting a new trail run tracking feature, which seems like an attempt to compete with Garmin more so than the Apple Watch Ultra line. It allows you to download GPX files for GPS routes to enable real-time navigation and elevation guidance. You’ll also get an estimated completion time and real-time hydration alerts. One note: The algorithm essentially predicts how much you’ve sweat based on workout intensity and demographic data — the sensors themselves aren’t measuring how many electrolytes or how much water you’ve actually lost. Divers also get IP69K, 10 ATM, and EN 13319 dust- and water-resistance rating, plus a bespoke diving app from scuba equipment maker Mares. The app will arrive later this year and will monitor descent speed, record time at a given depth, plus give ascent guidance.
The Galaxy Watch 9, which is seeing a $30 price bump to $379.99, is mostly the same as last year’s Galaxy Watch 8. The most notable difference is that the Watch 9 (and the Ultra 2) ditch Samsung’s proprietary Exynos chipset for Qualcomm Snapdragon Wear Elite. Presumably, this is to help with power efficiency and AI processing. (Qualcomm announced the chip earlier this year at Mobile World Congress as an “AI-wearable first” chipset.) This could be to perhaps boost Gemini performance, and one new update with Wear OS 7 is you’ll be able to raise to talk without using the Gemini wake word. Samsung says it’s also tuned Gemini so it won’t trigger when you lift your wrist to check the time. It’s hard to gauge any performance boosts at a hands-on; some of my colleagues noticed a slight latency while scrolling through screens, but that could easily be due to demo models and wonky connectivity. We’ll have to see how the watches fare under normal testing conditions.
Battery capacity gets a slight boost on both the 40mm and 44mm watches. The smaller watch gets a roughly 20 percent increase to a 390mAh battery, while the larger one gets a more modest bump from 435mAh to 445mAh. The straps are 17 percent lighter with a new “air pocket structure,” which allows for a gap between the fabric and wrist for what Samsung promises is a more comfy, breathable fit.
The bulk of the Galaxy Watch 9’s updates come in the form of four new preventive health metrics, which are also coming to the Ultra 2. The first is a Vitals feature. After a week of consecutive wear during sleep, the Samsung Health app will generate a baseline for blood oxygen, heart rate, heart rate variability, skin temperature, and respiratory rate. In the morning, you’ll get a proactive alert if any deviate from your baseline, alongside some tips on how to get back on track. This is basically a dupe of Apple’s Vitals feature, which was released with watchOS 11 in 2024.
It’s also adding a Heart Health Score and a Daily Cardio Load metric. The former generates a score out of 100 every day based on your eight-day sleep time average, moderate to vigorous activity level, BMI, and vascular load. The latter helps you balance training versus recovery based on workout intensity, maximum training load, and real-time heart rate data. The idea is to help you determine if you’re overtraining, undertraining, or doing just the right amount. Again, these aren’t new ideas. We’ve seen similar features from Oura, Whoop, and Fitbit (now Google Health) over the past few years.
The most unique health metric is the new Fitness Index. It’s a radar chart that graphs how your strength, flexibility, endurance, cardio, and body composition compare to other Samsung users, based on factors like your VO2 Max, heart rate, step counts, activity time, and bioimpedance analysis results. You might be most familiar with radar charts if you play roleplaying games — it doesn’t tell you whether your metrics are good or bad, but rather it’s a method for visualizing your relative strengths and weaknesses.
This generation of Samsung watches feels like a mix of catching up to rivals’ health features and refining what already works. That’s not the worst combination, except for the fact that all the watches are more expensive. The company has been slowly increasing the prices of its wearables over time — though geopolitical factors probably play some role in this year’s bumps, too. Even so, you never like to see prices go up.
The watches are available for preorder starting today and are expected to ship starting August 7th.

title: I almost forgot Samsung’s Z Flip 8 was a foldable
summary: Samsung's new Galaxy Z Flip 8 feels more like a regular phone than ever. It's thinner, lighter, and has a front screen you can do just about anything on. Whether that's a good or bad thing, I'm not quite sure yet. I spent three hours with Samsung's newest flip phone last week, and it doesn't […]
full_text:
Samsung’s new Galaxy Z Flip 8 feels more like a regular phone than ever. It’s thinner, lighter, and has a front screen you can do just about anything on. Whether that’s a good or bad thing, I’m not quite sure yet.
I almost forgot Samsung’s Z Flip 8 was a foldable
Cover screen? More like cover phone.
I spent three hours with Samsung’s newest flip phone last week, and it doesn’t look too different from last year’s Z Flip 7. It’s still got a 6.9-inch FHD+ AMOLED display on the inside. It’s still got a 4.1-inch Super AMOLED cover screen on the outside. It still starts at 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, and it still has a 4,300mAh battery. But this year Samsung has added even more features that make this thing a full-on phone while it’s closed.
For starters, Samsung has added three new gestures to the outer display. If you swipe down from the top left of the screen, you’ll see your notification tray. Swipe down from the top right, and you’ll get quick settings. Swipe up from the bottom, and you’ll get near a full-blown app drawer. If you wanted to use your closed phone for practically everything, that’s what Samsung is offering here.
Previously, you had to use Samsung’s Good Lock to launch apps on the cover screen, and while it worked, it was basically a workaround. Now this is a native feature. On first impression, it’s nice to have the option, but part of the magic of a flip phone, for me at least, has always been the limitations. If the Flip 8 is simply a phone, but in a small, square aspect ratio, will I still feel less motivated to doomscroll?
Samsung has also shaved a few fractions of a millimeter off this thing to make what it says is the thinnest and lightest flip phone on the market. The Z Flip 8 is just 13.1mm thick folded and 6.1mm thick unfolded, and weighs 180g. This is still thicker than Samsung’s own Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, which comes in at just 4.1mm unfolded, and it’s certainly still thicker than a regular phone while closed, but as far as flip phones go, it’s currently the one to beat.
This year’s phone has also been made thinner using Samsung’s new Flex Titanium display technology, which is also in its new Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra. Samsung says Flex Titanium shaves off thickness by using a thinner titanium film under the OLED, as well as a tighter bonding between the base plate and display module. In practice, I’m not sure you’re going to notice a fraction of a millimeter, but Samsung says this display is 20x more durable, which is sorely needed considering the amount of Z Flips with cracked inner displays I’ve seen while riding the subway.
New battery technology also had a part in enabling a thinner and lighter phone. Samsung has finally made the transition to silicon carbon — which allows for denser batteries than standard lithium ion — though it says it’s using less silicon than competitors for safety and longevity reasons. In the Flip 8, the capacity and charging speed are the same as the Flip 7, but it was able to make the cell physically smaller.
If you were hoping for a massive camera upgrade this year, you’re going to be disappointed, as the Flip 8 is sticking with the same camera hardware we saw in last year’s Flip 7. You’re still getting a 50MP main and 12MP ultrawide, which are fine enough, but don’t expect the 200MP main camera from the Z Fold 8 Ultra or even the 50MP ultrawide from the Z Fold 8. That said, Samsung has brought its impressive Super Steady Horizontal Lock feature to the phone.
Probably the coolest feature I tried during my three hours with the device was the new “Now Brief” widget generator, which can create Now Brief widgets to proactively show you information about your day. During my time with the device, Samsung demo’d asking the phone to show the pollen levels every morning, and the Flip 8 generated a custom UI showing the day’s pollen level. I’m eager to get my hands on the phone for a longer period to pressure-test this feature, as Samsung made it seem like you could ask for a huge variety of widgets. This feels very similar to Google’s recently announced Android 17 feature, but optimized for the front display of the Flip.
The Flip 8 is more expensive than last year. This year, it’s starting at $1,199.99, up from the Flip 7’s $1,099.99 starting price, for the same storage and RAM configurations. Just about everything is subject to the RAM apocalypse these days, but if you want a flip phone that’s more phone than ever in its closed state, the Flip 8 might be the one to get.
