title: What is Beijing thinking? Why Washington is struggling to understand its rival
summary:
After Donald Trump’s high-stakes summit with Xi Jinping in May, the idea of US-China “strategic stability” appeared in readouts from both sides.
While the White House framed this vision as a “constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of fairness and reciprocity”, Beijing said only that it was a “constructive bilateral relationship of strategic stability”.
China watchers zoomed in on the phrase – especially the Chinese version – debating what it could reveal or conceal about...
full_text:
What is Beijing thinking? Why Washington is struggling to understand its rival
Language is important in US-China diplomacy, but funding cuts and dwindling student exchanges have left a ‘major gap’ in capabilities
While the White House framed this vision as a “constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of fairness and reciprocity”, Beijing said only that it was a “constructive bilateral relationship of strategic stability”.
China watchers zoomed in on the phrase – especially the Chinese version – debating what it could reveal or conceal about Beijing’s long-term ambitions.
They put that down to funding cuts to language programmes in America as well as dwindling student exchanges and less interest in learning Chinese.
The result is a disjointed network of government programmes, think tanks and independent researchers seeking to translate and interpret China’s latest moves.
Analysts say that fragmentation could make it harder for Washington to understand its most critical bilateral relationship.

full_text:
Chile hunts for copper buyers beyond China with US$100 billion mining plan
Chile’s foreign minister says the copper market is too concentrated, but refining more at home means competing with Chinese smelters
Chile wants to widen the group of countries buying its copper and attract about US$100 billion in mining investment over the next decade, its foreign minister said on Wednesday, in the most explicit move yet by the new government in Santiago to reduce its exposure to Chinese demand.
“The market is highly concentrated and we need to broaden the number of places that buy our copper,” Francisco Perez Mackenna said at a Bloomberg summit in Singapore, part of a tour through the Asia-Pacific.
He said China would remain a very important client because of its industrial capacity, and that global demand should continue to grow further as investment in data centres accelerates.
The concentration he described has deepened rather than eased over the past decade, with China now consuming roughly 58 per cent of the world’s copper and taking more than half of Chilean shipments.
The South American country produced 5.3 million tonnes in 2025, about a quarter of global output, making it the largest producer and the supplier no major buyer can replace at short notice.
Central bank figures through June show that the dependence is uneven and falls almost entirely on unprocessed ore.

full_text:
US not getting enough critical minerals from China, Greer says as Xi-Trump meeting looms
Remarks on minerals vital for electronics come as Marco Rubio and Wang Yi discuss upcoming meeting of leaders
Washington is still not receiving sufficient critical mineral exports from China, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Wednesday, even as top American and Chinese officials met to finalise key economic deliverables for President Xi Jinping’s expected visit to the White House.
“We are getting a flow of critical minerals from China. It’s not as much as we would want. It’s not at the pace we would want, but we are getting them,” Greer said during his testimony before the Senate Finance Committee.
Greer also highlighted that the administration is holding “regular meetings and calls with Chinese officials at all levels” to follow through on its “commitment” to expedite export applications, and maintained that the US has “substantial leverage” to push for compliance.
“We have a variety of trade tools that we have used, and some are suspended, some are in effect, that we can use to make sure that they comply,” Greer added.
“But most importantly, we are accelerating domestic production to try to get away from that dependency.”

full_text:
How China and Indonesia can build a truly sturdy partnership
From handling business friction to aligning long-term goals, three practical steps can elevate ties beyond economic convenience
In April 1955, amid the Cold War, 304 representatives across 29 Asian and African nations convened in Bandung, Indonesia, to discuss the principles of a more complex future world order. Among them were India, China and host Indonesia.
Seven decades on from Bandung, China is the world’s second-largest economy while Indonesia is the largest economy in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), which is China’s top trading partner. China is Indonesia’s largest trading partner, and it has ranked among Indonesia’s top three investors for the last five years.
Such remarkable growth in ties inevitably comes with undercurrents that must be taken seriously. Indonesia recorded a US$20.5 billion trade deficit with China last year, and some view the surge in high-quality and affordable Chinese imports as displacing domestic producers, especially in the textile and manufacturing sectors.

Lawmakers called out China’s growing footprint at the United Nations on Wednesday as a vehicle for espionage even as a Congressional hearing over its funding descended into a heated partisan battle over the Iran war started by US President Donald Trump.

full_text:
Donald Trump has defended his new 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods, claiming the country cannot survive without the US.
The White House announced the sweeping round of import duties – due to come into effect next month – on Monday, igniting fresh tensions between Washington and Ottawa.
Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, said his country was “united” in the face of such threats. He spoke with Trump earlier on Tuesday.
“Canada has been very, very tough on us over the years, for many years, and no other president’s done anything about it,” the US president said in the Oval Office. “In all fairness to them, they need us to survive. Without us, there’s no way they can survive.”
Earlier this week, the White House said that the new levies were because Canada has unfairly discriminated against US cars, alcohol and dairy products. The tariffs will go into effect in 30 days, leaving time for possible discussions between the two countries.
Carney told reporters: “We agreed to intensify negotiations in the coming weeks, and the team and myself look forward to doing that.”
The tariffs will hit a wide range of products, the White House said, including wine, hockey sticks and cement. They also include goods previously protected from import taxes under the United States-Mexico-Canada (USMCA) agreement.
Trump told members of the press that the latest round of tariffs was not in response to the Canadian wildfire smoke that spread across North America last week.
On Friday, Trump blasted Canada for its response to the persistent wildfires and the smoke that affected about 109 million people across the midwest, mid-Atlantic and north-east.
“The cost is incalculable!” Trump raged on social media. “This is Willful Negligence, and becoming a yearly occurrence, costing the United States Billions of Dollars, which cost of this pollution must of necessity be added to the TARIFFS Canada is currently paying.”
However, the president told reporters on Tuesday that his administration was looking at those tariffs “separately”.

Australia is not ruling out stepping up joint patrols of the South China Sea following “destabilising” missile testing in the region, Australian Associated Press reports.
The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, was asked last night about the potential of more regular regional sea patrols in tandem with the United States and Japan, following China’s launching of nuclear-capable missiles.
“The maritime zone is critical to stability in the region so, when we have a conversation about the South China Sea, that is something I’m sure we should all keep in mind,” she told reporters in Manila where she is attending the Asean foreign ministers’ meeting.
“We are concerned about some of the aggression we are seeing, we are concerned about some of the destabilising conduct we are seeing, and the countries of the region have a choice to make about how we all respond to that.”
Wong met her Chinese counterpart Wang Yi on the sidelines of the talks on Tuesday evening to highlight her concerns.
“You speak about the importance of mutual understanding,’’ she said.
“I agree, and I expect we will discuss our concerns ... including around peace and stability in our region, safe and professional military conduct, and the importance of transparency and reassurance of intent.”
China’s foreign ministry hit back at Wong’s comments, saying Australia was not party to the South China Sea issue and had no right to intervene.
“China urges relevant countries to stop stirring up tension and inciting confrontation,” spokesman Lin Jian told a regular briefing in Beijing.
It came as Wong prepared to warn China in a speech today that Australia would not be bullied by Beijing as it builds up its military strength.
One in five skipping personal hygiene or cleaning products amid cost of living concerns
A survey of more than 2000 Australians has found 1 in 5 (20%) have skipped buying personal hygiene or cleaning products in the last 12 months to afford other essentials like food, housing and petrol.
Conducted by leading charity Good360 Australia, the research shows 1 in 3 Australians (35%) have experienced hygiene poverty at some point, with 1 in 10 falling into it for the first time this year. The problem is worsening and now reaches well into middle income Australia, including full-time workers.
The toll is serious and often hidden: 1 in 3 have avoided social situations, 1 in 3 have felt embarrassed, ashamed or experienced mental health impacts, and nearly 1 in 4 have delayed a doctor or dental appointment.
Alison Covington, founder and managing director of good360, said:
The findings of this research are deeply concerning. Hygiene poverty is no longer a problem at the margins, it cuts across our communities, impacting millions of Australians who are being forced to skip basic hygiene products to afford food, rent, housing and petrol.
It is not only Australians on the lowest incomes that are affected. Our research shows hygiene poverty now reaches full time workers and all types of families, extending well into middle income Australia.
The impacts are serious and often hidden, with major implications for personal health and wellbeing, as well as for our society and economy. People are withdrawing from social life, delaying medical appointments, even avoiding work or job interviews.
No one in a country like Australia should have to make these choices. Everyone deserves to live with dignity, and that starts with the basics.

title: Meta won’t have to face the next planned social media addiction trial
summary: Less than a week before Meta's lawyers were set to return to a Los Angeles courtroom, the plaintiff accusing the platform of inflicting harm dropped the case. Brought by 15-year-old Florida plaintiff going by initials R.K.C., the case was set to be the second in a set of bellwether trials meant to test legal arguments […]
full_text:
Less than a week before Meta’s lawyers were set to return to a Los Angeles courtroom, the plaintiff accusing the platform of inflicting harm dropped the case. Brought by 15-year-old Florida plaintiff going by initials R.K.C., the case was set to be the second in a set of bellwether trials meant to test legal arguments that social media giants allegedly broke the law by creating features that hooked and harmed teens.
Meta won’t have to face the next planned social media addiction trial
After settling with other social media companies, the plaintiff dropped his case.
After settling with other social media companies, the plaintiff dropped his case.
TikTok, Snap, and YouTube previously settled claims brought by R.K.C. for undisclosed amounts. “In light of the overall successful result of the litigation and his concerns about enduring a grueling weekslong trial, he has elected to withdraw his claims against Meta,” R.K.C.’s lawyers Emily Jeffcott and Rahul Ravipudi said in a statement. “He’s ready to close this chapter and focus on his recovery and engage in therapy as he aspires to have a normal life.” That means Meta got out of this case without having to pay a settlement. “The claims never held up, and this outcome makes clear that we will not back away from defending ourselves against baseless lawsuits,” Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said in a statement.
Meta got out of this case without having to pay a settlement
Multiple cases have already begun to test claims about social media companies allegedly misleading users about the safety of their products and inflicting harm. Meta and Google’s YouTube lost the first bellwether case tried at the courthouse, with a jury finding them to be negligent and ordering them to pay a total of $6 million in compensatory and punitive damages to the single plaintiff. Separately, a New Mexico jury ordered the company to pay a $375 million penalty, and the state is preparing for the next phase of trial seeking structural business changes.
There’s still seven more bellwether cases on deck in the California state courthouse in LA, and a separate set of cases pending in a federal court in Oakland. Meta, Tiktok, Snap, and YouTube settled with a school district that was set to be the first in that separate set of bellwether cases seeking money to cover mental health-related costs to students allegedly caused by their platforms. Meta is still set to face claims brought by state attorneys general in federal court next month, alleging that it illegally misled the public about harmful and allegedly addictive features.

title: Tesla’s revenues are bouncing back, but profits are still weak
summary: After a dismal two years of weakening demand, falling sales, and damage to its brand by Elon Musk's political activities, Tesla's road to recovery continues apace. On the heels of an impressive delivery report, the company released its earnings for the second quarter of 2026 - giving us the latest glimpse at the EV company […]
full_text:
After a dismal two years of weakening demand, falling sales, and damage to its brand by Elon Musk’s political activities, Tesla’s road to recovery continues apace. On the heels of an impressive delivery report, the company released its earnings for the second quarter of 2026 — giving us the latest glimpse at the EV company that Musk has said he wants to transform into a leader of AI and robotics.
Tesla’s revenues are bouncing back, but profits are still weak
Tesla is in negative free cash flow territory, as it increases its expenditures on major projects like AI infrastructure and robotics.
Tesla is in negative free cash flow territory, as it increases its expenditures on major projects like AI infrastructure and robotics.
Despite that mission, Tesla remains a car company. And in the second quarter, it sold an impressive 480,126 vehicles, about a 25 percent increase compared to the second quarter of 2025. (For a direct-to-consumer company like Tesla, deliveries are a proxy for sales.)
Tesla certainly did a good job shrinking its inventory, which is good for the balance sheet. But what about those numbers?
Tesla certainly did a good job shrinking its inventory, which is good for the balance sheet. But what about those numbers?
Tesla said it earned $1.11 billion in net income on $28.2 billion in revenue in the quarter that ended June 30th. That’s a 26 percent increase in revenue but a 5 percent increase in profits over the second quarter of 2025, when the company earned $1.17 billion in net income on $22.5 billion in revenue. Tesla exceeded revenue expectations from Wall Street, which assumed approximately $26.4 billion in revenue.
But there were still signs of trouble. The company reported negative free cash flow of $1.1 billion, a sign that Tesla’s operating revenues are insufficient to cover its capital expenditures. Basically, Tesla is spending more — on AI infrastructure, robotics, and manufacturing — than its earning on car sales and energy installations. Last year, some analysts predicted that negative free cash flow could trigger a steep drop in share price. (Tesla’s share price is down 14 percent so far this year.) The company said it had $43.5 billion in cash on hand, but its capital expenditures were up year over year 142 percent to $5.7 billion this quarter.
In a shareholder deck, Tesla said it “generated over $100B in revenue on a trailing twelve-month basis for the first time.” It also touted Cybercab production at its Gigafactory in Texas, and said Tesla Semi production “remains on track” at its Nevada facility later this year. And it said it began construction for its Optimus humanoid robot production at the factory in Fremont after decommissioning the assembly line for the Model S and X.
“Tesla is in its largest and most exciting period of investment,” the company states. “From here, there remains much hard work as we aim to revolutionize transportation, energy and productivity through our leading real-world AI. Scaling will be non-linear, and we are focused on long-term value creation. We’ve never been more optimistic about the future.”
Automotive gross margins, which measures revenue minus the direct cost of manufacturing the vehicle, remains an important number for Tesla. They fund the company’s multi-billion dollar investments in AI, autonomous driving, and robotics, while also providing a buffer for Tesla to slash vehicle prices when demand slumps.
In the second quarter, Tesla said its automotive gross margins were 16.3 percent, minus revenue from the sale of regulatory credits (a revenue stream that will soon cease to exist, after the Trump administration’s elimination of penalties for automakers who exceed emission standards). That’s up over the 15 percent margins in Q2 2025, but down from 19.2 percent in Q1 of this year.
Tesla’s energy business remained a bright spot for the company. It reported $3.1 billion in energy generation and storage revenue, a 13 percent increase over the same period in 2025.
The earnings report is the latest evidence that Tesla was starting to turn the corner on a dismal two years of declining sales and falling profits. It also comes as the company faces tough questions about its slow progress in expanding its robotaxi operations. Tesla’s autonomous vehicle project has fallen far short of Musk’s prediction of covering 50 percent of the US population by the end of 2025. The company recently launched robotaxi operations in two Florida cities, Orlando and Tampa, but a crowdsourced tracker shows only a handful of cars were available.
Tesla rolled out a new update to Full Self-Driving (v14 Lite) for its vehicle owners, bringing personalized driving preference learning to individual Teslas. But the number of crashes involving Tesla drivers using Autopilot and FSD continues to grow at an alarming rate, with Electrek reporting 207 crashes in May 2026 alone.

title: Senator Lummis: Ethics, other provisions in crypto Clarity Act to be further discussed
full_text:
Senator Lummis: Ethics, other provisions in crypto Clarity Act to be further discussed
Senator Cynthia Lummis, one of the lead negotiators on the bill, told CoinDesk she was "pleased" that the updated bill was ready for release.
- Having state attorneys general able to bring criminal or private cases under the Clarity Act's ethics provision was a "red line" for Republican negotiators, Senator Cynthia Lummis told CoinDesk.
- The ethics provision is likely to be discussed through the weekend, alongside a few other issues in the bill.
- A group of Democrats said earlier Wednesday they opposed the bill as-is.
The U.S. Senate's Digital Asset Market Clarity Act draft is still open to changes on a number of big-ticket items that include its government-ethics section, Senator Cynthia Lummis, one of the lead negotiators on the bill, said about the effort that's "finally" getting closer to passage with the release of the text.
The Senate's Judiciary, Ethics and Intelligence Committees all had input into the bill, Lummis told CoinDesk on Wednesday, and while the process has "been very difficult," the bill is ready for additional feedback.
"It's time to show everyone the fully integrated bill that we will be voting on, and get the feedback from the industry that's about to be regulated, as well as others," Lummis said. "So I'm pleased we've reached this point."
Lummis released an updated text of the Clarity Act earlier Wednesday that merged the bills passed by the Senate Banking and Agriculture Committees into one longer bill. The updated text is not likely to be the final version of the bill.
The bill's proposed conflict-of-interest limits for government officials' crypto involvement will continue to be discussed through the weekend, and some of the illicit finance provisions may also see further discussion, Lummis said.
Ethics has been the most important provision the industry and the broader Congress has waited for. Lummis said that the Republican negotiators on the bill had worked with Democrats "for weeks on end" but were at an impasse over the role of state attorneys general and whether they could bring criminal or private cases against any parties bound by the ethics provision.
"That was a bright red line for a lot of U.S. senators who did not want to subject themselves to being sued by a different state attorney general," Lummis said. "That was also true of the White House, which has been subject to multiple lawsuits and prosecutions by state attorneys general, and so that's kind of a bright line issue for a lot of senators, and certainly for the White House."
States could, instead, sue crypto exchanges that list any assets which would violate the ethics provision, Lummis said.
Beyond the president, the ethics agreement would apply to any other lawmaker, any high-level federal judge (including those on a district court, appeals court, the U.S. Supreme Court or the Court of International Trade) and their spouses, Lummis said.
President Donald Trump's crypto business ties include a memecoin company that issues a coin named for the president and a stablecoin issuer.
A group of Democrat Senators said in a statement late Wednesday that the bill still fell "short" of where it needed to be to get their support, but that they would keep working on it with Republicans. Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, argued Wednesday that the policy as written would let Trump continue his crypto businesses largely untouched, and any improper activity would be ignored by his loyal Department of Justice and then legally fenced off from prosecution once he leaves office.
Other outstanding issues
Beyond ethics, lawmakers may continue to negotiate over illicit finance provisions, Lummis said.
"We think we've landed in a good place," she said, because the effort addresses the Bank Secrecy Act, money-laundering protections, sanction coverage for exchanges and decentralized finance (DeFi).
Some of the new additions were made at the request of law enforcement, such as a provision addressing crypto automated teller machine (ATM) fraud.
There is also a safe harbor for crypto platforms to freeze funds if they suspect the assets are tied to suspicious transactions, particularly if those companies are cooperating with law enforcement, she said.
The text also includes a provision saying it is the "sense of Congress" that at least two of the commissioners on the Securities and Exchange Commission and Commodity Futures Trading Commission would be nominated in consultation with the minority party. Right now, neither agency has any Democratic commissioners, with the SEC helmed by three Republicans, while the CFTC just has a single commissioner running the agency.
Lummis said the hold-up on getting Democrats is on Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's end, as he needs to submit names to the White House.
"The language in there is not to compel the president to do something. It's basically to compel Senator Schumer to submit some names to the president," she said.
As of press time, it's also unclear when the bill may hit the Senate floor for a vote. Majority Leader John Thune's office told CoinDesk earlier Wednesday that he wants to bring the bill up soon, but Lummis noted that some of the Senate would be absent next week for Senator Lindsey Graham's funeral. The bill needs at least 60 votes to advance, and the Senate leaves town on August 7 for its summer recess.

title: Key Democratic lawmakers say crypto Clarity Act 'falls short' on ethics, other issues
full_text:
Key Democratic lawmakers say crypto Clarity Act 'falls short' on ethics, other issues
Several of the Democrats most likely to vote for the crypto market structure bill said they had issues with the new draft published by Republicans earlier in the day.
The newest draft of the crypto market structure bill "falls short" of where it needs to be on ethics and other provisions, a group of U.S. Senate Democrats said Wednesday.
Senators Angela Alsobrooks, Cory Booker, Catherine Cortez Masto, Ruben Gallego, John Hickenlooper, Mark Warner and Raphael Warnock — a core group of negotiators that would likely be needed to advance the bill — said in a joint statement shared with CoinDesk that they would keep working with their Republican counterparts on the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act (Clarity Act) but that it needed more work on various outstanding issues, including how the bill addresses illicit finance and consumer protections.
Alsobrooks and Gallego were the only lawmakers to vote for the Clarity Act in committee, while several others on the statement have expressed support for the bill in the past.
"The Republican-proposed text of the CLARITY Act as it currently stands falls short," the statement said. "Key provisions including those addressing ethics for elected officials, consumer protection, illicit finance, conflicts of interest and market integrity must be strengthened."
Senate Republicans published a new draft of the Clarity Act earlier Wednesday, including an ethics provision that the White House and President Donald Trump agreed to.
Senator Bernie Moreno, one of the lead Republicans on the bill, said in a post on X (formerly Twitter) earlier Wednesday that it was “the most powerful ethics language in U.S. history.”
“Don’t listen to the DC Democrat lies,” his post said.
The ethics provision has been an outstanding issue for over a year, stretching back to the Senate's work on the stablecoin-focused Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act last year, but the issue took on a renewed focus in recent weeks after Trump shared his latest financial disclosure showing he made over $1.4 billion from his crypto ventures in 2025.
It's unclear when the bill may hit the Senate floor, though Republican Majority Leader John Thune's office told CoinDesk that he's still planning on moving forward in the coming days.
The Senate leaves town after August 7 for the summer recess, and the Senate has other issues to take up as well. It will need 60 votes to advance, meaning as many as 10 Democrats may need to vote for the bill. "We have been working in good faith with our Republican colleagues for the past year and will continue doing so to get this over the finish line," the Democratic lawmakers said.

title: After shocking quarter, IBM insists that AI isn’t killing the mainframe
summary: After IBM's stock crashed last week on warnings of a poor mainframe sales, the CEO explained that AI wrecked corporate hardware budget, temporarily.
full_text:
On Wednesday, IBM officially reported earnings and the news was as bad as everyone knew it would be.
While the 115-year-old company still generates boatloads of cash — $17.2 billion in revenue, $9.9 billion in gross profit, nearly 58% margins, and $2.2 billion in net earnings for the quarter — its results fell well short of Wall Street’s expectations.
It was such a bad miss that IBM CEO Arvind Krishna and the board took an unprecedented step of warning investors ahead of time that the earnings was “was worse than our expectations,” offering everyone a sneak peek.
He published a “letter to investors,” last week sharing preliminary results. It warned of abysmal revenue in the company’s all-important “infrastructure” category and said that profit margins were also going to take a hit. The company’s stock instantly tanked 25%, it’s biggest single-day decline ever. Until then, the stock had performed well under Krishna’s six years of leadership, buoyed by the AI data center boom that had been lifting all boats.
On Wednesday, IBM also lowered its full-year growth forecasts, meaning this horrible quarter would impact the rest of the year. The culprit? IBM’s cash-cow mainframe business was down 42%.
That’s a cascading problem, because as CFO Jim Kavanaugh explained on the quarterly call with investors, IBM earns $3 in software revenue for every $1 of mainframe hardware it sells.
However, the CEO and CFO spent the call insisting that this was a temporary blip and all would be well soon.
What happened, they said, was that “tens” of customers that were due to buy a new mainframe during the quarter, opted not to do so. That may not sound like a lot of customers, but mainframes are systems that cost hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars, and with maintenance contracts and software, generate many millions more.
The same AI boom that lifted IBM’s boat, also sank it.
Instead of buying a new mainframe, these clients bought other hardware, Krishna explained. They were faced with astronomically high cost increases of 15% to 30% for data center gear and PCs.
“When they were faced with that issue, then they decided to move budget to those areas where they were having that extreme price,” Krishna said.
Enterprise hardware makers like Dell and HP have warned that rising costs on components like memory, caused by the AI build-out boom, have forced them to raise prices. Apple has said the same.
But Krishna promised that those customers will still buy their new mainframes eventually — along with their new software contracts. In fact, he said some of them have already done so this quarter. “We see no evidence of clients moving off the mainframe,” he said.
We’ll have to wait and see. But the tech industry has predicted the death of the mainframe for many decades now. Maybe even AI won’t kill it.

title: Sales were up at Tesla but so were costs and spending
summary: Q2 2026 was profitable, but barely.
full_text:
Tesla posted its financial statement for the second quarter of the year this afternoon. Earlier in July, we learned that the American automaker had had a good quarter in terms of sales, growing 25 percent year over year. Fans hoping that sales increase would result in a plenty profitable Tesla may be disappointed, though. Revenues are up but so are expenses, and the company’s once-enviable double-digit profit margin has fallen to just 1.4 percent.
Tesla brought in $20.5 billion from its electric vehicle business, a 23 percent increase year over year, and just $146 million came from automotive regulatory credits. Credits have been a key to Tesla’s profitability in previous challenging quarters, but they were abolished in the United States with Musk’s blessing in 2025.
There was growth from its energy and storage business, which grew 13 percent year over year to revenues of $3.1 billion, but the most growth was in Tesla’s services, which doubled, bringing in $4.6 billion. Tesla’s shift from a one-time purchase to a monthly subscription for its much-criticized FSD partially automated driver assist—something tied to CEO Elon Musk’s gargantuan remuneration package—was a big help here.
Overall, total revenues were up 26 percent, to $28.2 billion.
But the cost of doing business went up more. Tesla’s operating expenses went up 47 percent to $4.4 billion, and income from those operations fell by 57 percent year over year to $398 million. The company is still profitable—it generated $1.1 billion for the quarter, but that’s 5 percent less than the same three months last year.

title: Hope for thousands of MS patients as 'life-changing' drug now on NHS in England
summary: Fampridine boosts nerve signals to make it easier to walk, with up to 5,000 eligible.
full_text:
Hope for thousands of MS patients as 'life-changing' drug now on NHS in England
- Published
The first drug to help people with multiple sclerosis walk is being made available on the NHS in England.
Fampridine boosts nerve signals to make it easier for some people to move and live independently.
Aysen Slack, who used to pay for fampridine privately until it became too costly, said the decision would make a "huge difference".
Up to 5,000 people in England could benefit each year. The drug is already available elsewhere in the UK.
Multiple sclerosis is caused by the immune system attacking the protective covering around nerve cells - known as myelin.
This damage impairs the ability of nerves to carry electrical messages from the brain to the rest of the body - including those needed for the precise control of muscles needed to walk.
Fampridine is known as a "signal booster" as it helps those electrical messages still get through.
Clinical trials showed around four in 10 people taking the drug had improvements in their walking speed and in how long they could walk for.
This could be the difference between getting around the house or needing help at home or enabling people to go out and see friends and family.
Current NHS support includes physiotherapy and walking aids.
The drug has previously been rejected for use by the NHS in England as it was not considered value for money, although it did become available in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
'Clear benefit'
Aysen Slack, 65 and from Eastbourne, chose to pay privately for the pills once she heard about them.
She said fampridine was "working well for me" but came at a "significant expense and I could not keep doing that forever" so she had to stop.
Slack said it was "great news" the drug was coming to the NHS and she "would definitely like to try" again.
"My mobility has decreased a lot and even in my flat I have to use sticks now," she said, "it would make a huge difference to my life if I were able to improve my walking."
More than 120,000 people live with MS in England. However, only around 5,000 people a year will be eligible - based on the extent of their walking difficulties.
Patients will try the medicine for up to a month and only those showing "clear benefit" will be able to continue taking it.
Prof Frankie Swords, the NHS national medical director, said: "Walking difficulties can have a huge impact on the freedom and independence of people with MS, so this signal-boosting pill could be life-changing for thousands of patients.
"Even a modest improvement could mean getting around the house more easily, going out with greater confidence and living more independently."
Ceri Smith, from the MS Society, said they were "delighted" by the news as the drug could be "life-changing" for many, allowing people to "live more independently or stay in employment".
- Published27 September 2025

title: Rain to return this weekend as parts of UK on brink of drought
summary: Following weeks of mainly dry weather, we can welcome some rain this weekend, but it is not going to be that much, as Chris Fawkes explains.
full_text:
Rain to return this weekend as parts of UK on brink of drought
- Published
If you cannot remember the last time it rained, you are probably not alone.
June was actually wetter than average in the UK, which might come as a surprise given our recent run of weather, but for England and Wales the majority of that rain came down in the first two weeks of the month.
Since 15 June, most of England has recorded less than 10mm of rain with large areas of central southern England seeing 3mm or less. Meanwhile, Wisley in Surrey has had no rain at all for 36 consecutive days.
Most of Wales has seen less than 25mm (1in) of rain since the middle of June, but it has been particularly dry in the north-east with Rhyl in Denbighshire recording only 3mm.
A Thames Water hosepipe ban came into force on Thursday, adding to other bans already in place for customers of other water companies across the south of the UK, as parts of southern, central and eastern England were declared to be close to drought.
Northern Ireland had a very wet June, recording 67% more rain than average, and it was also very wet in western Scotland. However, July has been much drier than average in Northern Ireland and most of Scotland, though the rain has continued in the Highlands, with Aultbea already reaching the July average rainfall, and with more on the way.
- Is there a hosepipe ban in my area? What you need to know - Published14 hours ago
 
- Parts of the UK move closer to drought - Published1 day ago
 
Rain on the way this weekend
This weekend will bring a change in our weather patterns.
Normally weather systems move eastwards with time. However, the high pressure we have had for a long time now is actually going to move westward, in something known as retrogression.
This will allow the jet stream to move right over the UK and steer weather fronts in, bringing some welcome rain.
The hills of Northern Ireland, northern England and north Wales will have 5-10mm of rain this weekend.
Western Scotland will be wetter, with 10-20mm over high ground.
The rain is likely to be lighter and patchier in the Midlands, southern and east England with just a few millimetres expected and some areas could miss out altogether.
In the grand scheme of things the rain is not that much, but could double the amount we have seen since mid-June in some areas.
While it may bring some relief to parched gardens, it will not be enough to stop a slide towards more widespread drought conditions.
Next week, rain looks to be concentrated in the north-west of the UK, and perhaps very wet in the Highlands late in the week. Little, if any, rain is expected in the south and east.
Beyond that, into August, there could be another heatwave forming in Spain and France, though it's too soon to tell whether that will reach the UK.
Keep up to date with the latest for your area on the BBC Weather website or app.
Boiling Point: The Week of Extreme Heat
The last week of June 2026 saw record-breaking temperatures across parts of the UK and Europe. While some enjoyed the sunshine, the heat caused trains, schools and emergency services to buckle.

title: Glasgow set to welcome the world for scaled back Commonwealth Games
summary: Athletes from 74 countries and territories will compete for 215 gold medals over 10 days of competition.
full_text:
Glasgow set to welcome the world for scaled back Commonwealth Games
- Published
When the fastest man on the planet won Commonwealth relay gold for Jamaica in 2014, more than 50,000 fans cheered him home at Hampden.
But the athletes seeking to emulate Usain Bolt when the Games return to Glasgow - including mile world record holder Josh Kerr - will be competing at Scotstoun Stadium in front of 11,000 spectators.
This time round almost everything is on a smaller scale but organisers are confident fans will create a Tartan Army-style atmosphere for the 3,000 competitors who will be chasing glory.
From Friday until 2 August, 215 gold medals will be up for grabs - compared to 261 when Scotland last staged the Games - but Glasgow 2026 will see a record 47 para-sports events.
The action gets under way with bowls and para-bowls heats at 09:30, but the Games will be officially opened by King Charles during a ceremony at the Hydro later.
It will be attended by athletes from 74 nations and territories as well as dignitaries including Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Scotland's First Minister John Swinney and the First Minister of Wales Rhun ap Iorwerth.
Some of the 4,000 Games volunteers, aged 16 to 96, will also take part in the celebration.
Why is Glasgow hosting the Games?
Glasgow stepped in when the Australian state of Victoria pulled out of hosting the Games in July 2023.
It had only agreed to stage the event in April 2022 after the Commonwealth Games Federation (CGF) struggled to find a host.
Organisers had originally estimated the event would cost A$2.6bn (£1.35bn) and the state government had billed it as a boost for the regions.
But the projected bill soared to more than A$6 billion (£3.11bn).
Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews said the new figure was "more than twice the estimated economic benefit" it would bring to the state.
The decision not only plunged the future of the 2026 edition into doubt but the Games as whole.
But in September 2024 a deal, backed by the Scottish government, was agreed for Glasgow to host "a scaled back, but high-quality" event.
It will be staged across four venues along an eight-mile stretch - Scotstoun Stadium, Tollcross International Swimming Centre, Glasgow International Arena and the Scottish Event Campus (SEC).
In 2014 the budget for the Games was £543m but no public money has been spent on the 23rd edition, which will cost £150m in total.
The CGF is investing £100m of this, with the remainder coming from commercial revenue streams such as ticketing, sponsorship, broadcast rights and merchandise.
Athletics, cycling and swimming have proved the most popular but tickets are still available for many events.
Who is competing in Glasgow?
The triumphant 2012 London Olympics were still fresh in the mind when Glasgow last staged the Commonwealth Games.
Usain Bolt topped an athletics cast list which also included Olympic champions David Rudisha of Kenya (800m), Australia's Sally Pearson (100m hurdles) and Valerie Adams of New Zealand (shot put).
This year the most decorated track star is also a Jamaican sprinter.
Elaine Thompson-Herah made her Commonwealth debut in 2014 and went on to become the first woman in history to win back-to-back Olympic 100m and 200m titles in Rio and Tokyo.
She is aiming to defend the titles she won at Birmingham 2022.
Other big names include Canadian sprinter Andre De Grasse, who is a double Olympic champion, and two-time world 200m champion Shericka Jackson of Jamaica.
Meanwhile, Scotland's Eilish McColgan will be hoping to retain her Commonwealth title in the 10,000m.
Her triumph four years ago followed her mother Liz's victory in the same event at the 1986 Games in Edinburgh.
McColgan will line-up alongside compatriot Megan Keith, who broke the European 10k road record in Spain earlier this year.
Meanwhile, reigning 1500m Commonwealth champion Laura Muir will run the 5,000m.
In the pool, South Africa's Chad Le Clos was one of the biggest draws in 2014 after he defeated his hero, American legend Michael Phelps, in the 200m butterfly at the London Olympics.
Le Clos will return to Glasgow, where he won two golds in 2014, with the aim of becoming the most decorated male in the history of the Games by adding to his current haul of 18 medals.
- Is Glasgow ready for the Commonwealth Games - and does the city care? - Published5 days ago
 
- Hoy backs Glasgow 2026 for 'massive success' - Published5 days ago
 
Fellow Olympic champions competing at Tollcross include Mollie O'Callaghan of Australia, England's Adam Ramsay-Peaty and Daniel Wiffen of Northern Ireland.
Duncan Scott, Scotland's most successful Olympian, will hope to add to his collection of 13 Commonwealth medals.
But Archie Goodburn, who has terminal brain cancer, could provide one of the moments of the Games if he lands a podium finish in the 50m breaststroke.
Last month he told BBC Scotland: "I get goosebumps thinking about it."
Elsewhere, two five-time Commonwealth champions will be hoping to delight the home crowd.
Bowls great Alex "Tattie" Marshall will be making his eighth Games appearance and para-cycling star Neil Fachie will retire after riding both men's tandem events.
What's new for 2026?
The mile returns to the Games for the first time since the 1966 edition in Kingston, Jamaica.
The race on 1 August - which will replace the 1500m - will see a stellar line-up go head-to-head over the distance made famous by Sir Roger Bannister.
In May 1954 he became the first person to run a mile in under four minutes and later that summer won gold over the same distance at the 1954 Games.
Fast forward 72 years and the line-up will include three Scots with high hopes of a medal.
Josh Kerr, fresh from breaking the 27-year-old mile world record in London, will be a favourite to top the podium.
But the former 1500m world champion will face competition from 2022 world champion Jake Wightman and Neil Gourley, who has world and European indoor 1500m medals to his name.
Australian track sensation Cameron Myers - who ran the fastest 1500m by an under-21, external in July - will also compete in the event.
In the women's mile race Scotland will be represented by Jemma Reekie.
The decision to scale back the Games meant there was some disappointment when the final schedule was announced.
Hockey was dropped despite a £5m national hockey centre being built for Glasgow 2014.
The cycling programme, which previously included mountain biking and road races, will be confined to the track.
In gymnastics, there is no room for any rhythmic events, with only artistic gymnastics being included.
Bowls, which were last time held at Kelvingrove, will be staged indoors at the SEC.
Badminton and squash were also scrapped and there will be no diving competitions.
What happened with the baton relay?
In 2014 the baton relay visited 70 Commonwealth nations and territories over 248 days, covering a distance of 190,000km (118,060 miles).
The epic journey concluded with a 40-day trip across Scotland involving 4,000 baton bearers.
They included actor Brian Cox, Scotland manager Gordon Strachan, singer Susan Boyle, broadcaster Kirsty Wark and cycling legend Sir Chris Hoy.
This time round each competing team was given its own baton to decorate rather than transporting one across the Commonwealth.
The Scottish leg of the relay was launched on 1 July when swimmer Duncan Scott sailed up the River Clyde on a power boat.
Since then the baton has travelled to communities, events, and festivals across the country's 32 local authorities.
Who will perform at the opening ceremony?
Celtic Park staged a spectacular opening ceremony in 2014 which featured Rod Stewart, dancing Tunnock's Tea Cakes and a Red Arrows fly over.
This year the event will be staged at the Hydro and will feature performances by headliner KT Tunstall, Callum Beattie, Nathan Evans, Tom Walker and Saint Phnx.
Inspiration for the opening ceremony has come from a variety of sources, including Bad Bunny's half-time show at this year's Supe

title: Most sewage spills in England may be illegal, new research suggests
summary: The new analysis from a prominent water campaigner emerged after secret court documents were leaked.
full_text:
Most sewage spills in England may be illegal, new research suggests
- Published
Most of the sewage spills into England's waterways in the last two years may have been illegal but gone unpunished, according to new analysis.
UK law states that raw sewage should not be released during "normal" weather conditions, yet until now the regulator has not clarified exactly what that means.
But campaigner Prof Peter Hammond obtained a definition in secret court papers, and said it shows that for more than 80% of the time sewage was being spilled, the weather was "normal" - making the spills possibly illegal.
The water companies and the regulator, the Environment Agency (EA), rejected the analysis and said they were working to reduce spill numbers.
- Failing water sector needs stronger regulation, says damning review - Published3 June 2025
 
- Record number of illegal sewage spills in Windermere last year - Published31 March 2025
 
The last few years have seen growing awareness and mounting public anger at the amount of raw sewage that is being discharged into England's rivers, lakes and seas.
The country's sewage issues are, in large part, caused by the fact that drains usually take rainfall into the same network of pipes that remove waste from homes.
This means that when it rains, if there is not enough spare capacity, the system and sewage treatment works can be quickly overwhelmed.
But until now, it has not been clear what amount of rainfall there must be before water companies can legally spill raw sewage into waterways. Campaigners have said this has allowed the industry to spill routinely with no consequences.
Secret court documents
Earlier this year, a source at the EA sent Prof Hammond undisclosed documents from a court case against Southern Water for illegal sewage spilling in 2021.
It included a previously undisclosed definition of "heavy rain" conditions. And accompanying internal EA documents confirmed that water companies can spill sewage when there is "heavy" rain i.e. beyond the "normal" weather conditions.
Prof Hammond, a retired academic and campaigner whose work on sewage spills has been cited in Parliament and in economic regulator Ofwat's enforcement decisions, used the definition to run an analysis of water company spill data.
He looked at more than 350 storm overflow outlets in England and whether there had been heavy rain when they were spilling sewage.
The outlets include all of the largest sewage treatment works and a representative selection of smaller ones, across all England's nine water companies serving more than 30m people.
Hammond said he found about 86% of the raw sewage spilling hours took place when there had not been heavy rain, meaning those discharges could be potentially illegal.
None of England's water companies did well in Hammond's analysis, with even the best having a potential illegality rate of over 70% for the last two years.
"It's totally outrageous, both from the point of the water companies who are exploiting the weak regulation but also from the Environment Agency's point of view, where they've not been doing their job properly," Prof Hammond told BBC News.
The EA told BBC News that the "heavy rain" definition Hammond was using was only for the Southern Water sites and that different parts of England had different levels of rainfall, so different thresholds.
Hammond said he had also run his analysis taking into account regional variations in rainfall and it had not significantly changed the level of possible illegality, because most of the spills took place at relatively low levels of rain.
EA inaction
It is not the first time the Environment Agency's enforcement regime has been called into question.
In 2024, the Office for Environmental Protection (OEP), an independent public body, ruled that the EA was not applying legislation properly as to when sewage could be legally discharged. It said the EA was allowing water companies to spill in "normal" weather rather than "exceptional circumstances" - as the law states.
In light of the OEP report the EA issued new guidance last year, external making it clear that spills should not take place during normal weather.
But in an email exchange with the BBC the EA refused to confirm that spills should only take place during "exceptional circumstances", but said it would "always take action" if there had been a breach of the law.
"However, to meet the strict legal requirements needed to pursue a criminal conviction we must consider a wide range of factors including specific site and permit conditions, as well as rainfall totals," its spokesperson said.
Asked to provide details of completed or ongoing enforcement action related to spills in "normal" weather a spokesperson for the EA said they could not, citing "ongoing legal proceedings".
In response to Prof Hammond's analysis, a spokesperson for Water UK, which represents the water companies, told the BBC: "As confirmed by the High Court and the Office for Environmental Protection, discharges should only occur in 'exceptional circumstances' or if preventing them is technically possible but would involve excessive cost.
"In any case, we want to end all discharges and are working to end them as fast as we physically can."

title: Airport drop-off fees up by a third - here are the priciest
summary: The cost of parking closest to the terminal just for a few minutes has hit £10 at two of the UK's busiest airports.
full_text:
Airport drop-off fees up by a third - here are the priciest
- Published
Drop-off fees at the UK's major airports have risen by a third on average since last summer, new analysis has found.
The RAC looked at the cost of pulling up at the closest point to terminals at the 20 busiest airports - 16 had put up their fees since last year.
Two London airports, Gatwick and Stansted, topped the price table at £10.
Trade body Airports UK said free drop-offs were available and fees were part of airports' business models and climate change objectives.
London Gatwick's is the highest "farewell fee", charging £10 for 10 minutes on the forecourt outside either of its terminals. At Stansted, £10 buys a more generous 15 minutes, at "Express Set Down" outside departures.
London City Airport, which only started making people pay this year, is the most expensive on a per-minute basis. Its £8 charge for five minutes works out at £1.60 per minute.
In contrast, none of the top 10 airports in the EU charge for drop-offs, according to RAC research.
The RAC acknowledged UK airports generally offered other options for dropping people off at locations further from the terminal, sometimes with free shuttle buses.
But the motoring organisation's senior policy officer Rod Dennis said "having a captive audience should be no excuse for these 'farewell fees' – especially when they're completely at odds with how major airports around the world operate."
He said drivers needed to be especially careful of barrierless 'park now, pay later' drop-off zones, as they could face a parking charge notice if they failed to pay online or by phone within a certain period of time.
Gatwick's price hike comes as the airport tries to get more people arriving by trains and buses.
When the Transport Secretary approved the airport's plans for a second runway, one of the requirements was to have 54% of passengers using public transport.
Heathrow may also have to act to try and put people off driving to get a third runway.
A London Gatwick spokesperson said drop-off charges were aimed at disincentivising 'kiss and fly' trips and data indicated it was "influencing passengers to seek alternative options".
The airport links to 120 train stations across London and the South East, with eight local bus routes running 24/7, they said.
Passengers can still be dropped off for free at long-stay car parks, with a free shuttle bus to the terminal and Blue Badge holders are exempt from the charge, they said.
A spokesperson for Airports UK said where drop off fees are charged they are "necessary to manage congestion, and the traffic and air pollution concerns of our local communities, as well as our climate change objectives".
"These are issues that airports are mandated to manage by the government and local authorities," they said.
But Clive Wratten, CEO of the Business Travel Association, said fees were adding to businesses' costs.
"First it was environmental [reasons]. Then congestion management. Then funding new routes. Now apparently it is about offsetting tax rises," he said.
"The goalposts have moved so many times now that the credibility of any justification has long since gone."
How to avoid unexpected charges
- Check fees and how to pay them before setting off. Blue Badge holders are sometimes exempt. 
- Look for cheaper or free alternatives, for example car parks slightly further away which have shuttle buses to the terminal. 
- Research possible public transport alternatives. 
- Keep an eye on the time; make your goodbyes quick to avoid over-staying the limit. 
- Check where a taxi will drop you and whether they include the fee in their fare.

title: Why the UK is dithering over what to do about e-scooters
summary: Why is it taking so long for the government to regulate them, and what are the consequences of delay?
full_text:
When I step out of Southampton Central railway station, it takes me just seconds to spot an e-scooter. In this city, these devices have become a normal part of the transport ecosystem, along with e-bikes.
"It's just the most convenient way to commute from home to the station and back," says Keith Reed, who I speak to as he arrives at the station to catch a train to London. Keith says uses rental e-scooters twice a week. His alternative option would be his bike, but he'd then have to worry about where to leave it.
Around the city, there are parking areas for bright orange rental devices everywhere - but they're not necessarily a permanent feature. Southampton hosts one of the numerous government-backed trials around England. This one has been going on since 2021.
It also doesn't take long to find e-scooters which aren't part of the trial, but instead are owned by individuals. I see a man riding one along the pavement outside a parade of shops. He doesn't want to stop and talk.
These privately owned e-scooters are illegal to ride on public roads across the UK, but they've proliferated regardless. One expert told me the situation was a "Wild West".
Among people I spoke to in Southampton, the same concerns came up time and time again: "They're a blinking nuisance," says elderly pedestrian Fred. Another shopper, Martin, says he's "very concerned" whenever he sees them racing through precincts: "An accident's almost inevitable."
The endgame of the trials is to reach a decision on whether to make permanent hired e-scooter schemes such as the one Keith uses - and whether to bring in legislation that would legalise and regulate privately owned e-scooters too.
But six years since the trials started around England, there's still no conclusion - and as the UK government has responsibility for road traffic legislation across Great Britain, officials in Scotland and Wales say they are waiting on Westminster to act.
So why is it taking so long for the government to decide what to do, and what are the consequences of delay? What does the evidence tell us about how safe these things are?
And why are people using them in the first place - are they here to stay as a useful part of the transport offer, or will they end up being viewed as a pest on our streets?
What are e-scooters - and who rides them?
You'd recognise an e-scooter if you saw one. The Department for Transport's (DfT's) definition of an e-scooter includes no pedals, two wheels and a maximum continuous power rating of 500W.
And so far, the trials around England appear to have proved popular. According to DfT research, fom January 2022 to May 2024, 36.9 million trips were made across 30 trial areas outside of London. On average, nearly 19,500 e-scooters were available to hire every day.
Dr Yasir Ali, a reader in Transport Modelling at Loughborough University, says e-scooters are "complementary" to other modes of transport, rather than replacing them. Due to factors such as range and being exposed to the elements, they are less suitable for longer trips, rural areas with less infrastructure or in bad weather. They work best as "a first- and last-mile solution" in urban areas, to reduce reliance on cars for short trips.
Shared mobility charity CoMoUK's 2025 report suggests that for more than half of the people using rental e-scooters, the most common use was travelling to work or school. Its analysis of DfT data suggests the majority of people using hired e-scooters are male and under 35.
"Sometimes it's a bit difficult to take the bus from dot to dot", says Yan Zhang, who works at Southampton university and doesn't drive, "so for shorter distances, I'll take the scooter."
Around half of respondents to CoMoUK's online survey used it in conjunction with another mode of transport - such as riding to a railway station, like Keith.
Earlier evidence from a national evaluation of the trials published in 2022 found that although some users would have driven instead had they not had access to an e-scooter, the biggest "modal shift" - meaning switch in ways of getting around - to e-scooters was from walking. Given walking is an active mode of travel, this has raised questions over how significant the public health impact of e-scooter use really is.
And the usage of privately owned e-scooters isn't reflected in this research. The DfT has said between 760,000 and 1.2 million people in England aged 16 and over own one - despite the fact that it remains illegal to ride them in public.
In the eyes of the law, e-scooters are classed as motor vehicles. Outside of the trials, they can't be insured, and thus can only legally be ridden on private land, with the owner's permission.
The trials themselves are bound by strict rules. The devices' top speed is limited. Businesses who operate the pilots must insure them. Users must have a full or provisional driving licence, and they must not ride on the pavement. Helmets are recommended but not mandatory.
Richard Dilks, CEO of CoMoUK says "mass-scale use of something that is inherently low-carbon, low-impact, low-cost" is a "good thing" but "we also don't have rules of engagement about how they should be ridden".
And as a result of the delays in introducing regulation, Loughborogh University's Yasir Ali says "we are increasingly in a situation where the law and reality have diverged", with "the disadvantages of e-scooter use without securing the full benefits of regulation".
Against the law
Back in Southampton, I meet a lady pushing a black e-scooter, who doesn't want to give her name. She says nobody told her when she bought it that it was illegal to ride on the streets.
The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency has a unit that carries out surveillance of retailers to check they're complying with the law. But earlier this month, an investigation by the Press Association news agency discovered some retailers were advertising them for commuting purposes.
Police tell me they regularly see children illegally riding private e-scooters. Margaret Winchcomb, deputy executive director at the Parliamentary Advisory Council for Transport Safety (PACTS), says some are being specifically marketed at kids.
So what can police do? Forces regularly launch crackdowns where they seize illegally used devices, and often crush them. Each year, awareness campaigns run urging parents not to buy their kids an e-scooter for Christmas. But enforcement is a challenge.
Insp Matt Boiles from Avon and Somerset's road policing team says problems arise even with the legal trial devices - for example, people riding them after drinking alcohol, which counts as drink-driving. Riding with another person on the back is another common issue.
But officers see private e-scooters being illegally ridden in public places "all the time, every single day" and they can be really hard to catch - it isn't always safe for police in a car to pursue someone on an e-scooter, he says.
Insp Boiles despairs over parents buying them for children: "We do have parents attend a police station quite a lot, getting very, very upset that their child's £500 e-scooter has been seized." But "the legislation is really, really clear that you can't have it back".
How safe are they?
For many the biggest concern is safety.
There's a potential risk of fire if unregulated devices with lithium batteries are left to charge unattended. Most train operators have banned e-scooters on board for this reason.
But there's also the fact that riders are unprotected in the case of falling off or being hit by motorised vehicles. And - along with e-bikes - they can end up involved in collisions where pedestrians are hurt. Many trial e-scooters in the UK are restricted to 12.5mph, but privately owned scooters' speeds aren't.
Some coroners have even raised concerns. In 2022, a coroner in London called for action after the death of 14-year-old Fatima Abukah on a privately owned scooter.

title: Even camels can't cope: Africa's ships of the desert hit by rising temperatures
summary: Herders and experts tell the BBC how Africa's camels are suffering because of extreme heat.
full_text:
Even camels can't cope: Africa's ships of the desert hit by rising temperatures
- Published
Camels are famously known as the ships of the desert, but even these hardy animals are not being spared from the extremes of rising temperatures in Africa.
The Afar region of north-eastern Ethiopia is one of the hottest and driest places on Earth, where nomads often lead camel caravans carrying salt through the desert.
"I can see my camels suffering from extreme heat," Ali Umer, a camel herder from Semera in Afar, told the BBC.
"They get blisters on their feet, their eyes become watery and the hot sand burns their skin and eats up their hair when they are sitting," said the 40-year-old who owns around 500 camels.
"Within the past one month I have lost eight camel calves because of the extreme heat, it has become much more intense and difficult.
"Even the wind, which used to bring cool air, now carries heat," he said, adding he had noticed these drastic changes in the temperature in recent years.
He is not alone in his observations: scientists, animal welfare workers and various studies all mention stress, fatigue, dehydration, disease prevalence as direct impacts of extreme heat.
The higher temperatures also indirectly make camels suffer by causing severe loss of water, vegetation, and reduced shaded areas.
North Africa and the Horn of Africa host around 80% of the world's largest population of dromedary camels - those with one hump.
Over the years, farmers and cattle herders in these regions have switched to these animals because of their resilience to harsh heat and drought conditions.
But a study based on the perception of camel herders in southern Ethiopia, published in 2025, , externalshowed that high temperatures and climate variability had had a detrimental impact on camel herd health.
"Respondents reported that climate change and variability have affected camels' health, productivity, and reproductive performance," it said.
In neighbouring Somalia, the situation appears to be more serious. Research published in June, external has shown that drought-related camel mortality is a widespread crisis, affecting nearly 46% of camel-owning households.
The study included nearly 6,000 pastoral households and showed that the mortality was concentrated in northern regions, with Sool reporting a "staggering mortality rate of nearly 73%".
Extreme heat is the main cause behind the drought in the region although other factors like inadequate veterinary services and animal management make things worse, experts say.
An analysis by atmospheric scientists, external found that high temperatures in the region were behind the 2021-22 drought, as extreme heat makes water from soil and water bodies turn into vapour and plants release water in them into air as vapour.
Veterinarians say they are treating more sick camels and are seeing more deaths due to extreme heat and drought.
"We are seeing significant increase in cases of hyperthermia in camels as a result of which they get multiple infections," Hassan Nuya Guyo, a veterinary officer in Marsabit county in north-eastern Kenya bordering Ethiopia, told the BBC.
"In the last two years, we have seen a more than 15% increase in camel deaths in our county due to extreme heat."
Disease prevalence among camels and reduced milk yield from them are as a result of climate change impacts including heat stress, according to another study conducted in the Horn of Africa, external.
A similar story is playing out in North Africa. A study in Algeria, external, published this year, has shown a significant increase in camel deaths during summer heatwaves.
"Time series analysis highlights significant seasonal mortality patterns, underscoring the need for targeted interventions during high-risk periods like peak summer months; such as strategic water provisioning, supplemental feeding, and enhanced disease monitoring," it said.
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says extreme heat events have become a common phenomenon in several North African countries with heatwaves having increased with a clear upward trend since 1981.
It said a number of countries in the region and the Middle East reported temperatures above 50C in 2024.
WMO's State of the Climate in Africa 2025 report, external said North Africa recorded the most rapid warming of the six subregions - 0.43C per decade - between 1991 and 2025.
Experts say camels comfortably beat the heat up to around 40C by mainly allowing their body temperature to fluctuate by several degrees throughout the day to deal with outside temperature.
By doing that they avoid sweating and, combined with concentrated urine and dry faeces, it helps them minimise water loss, while their thick skin coat helps them ward off solar radiation.
"But camels can also experience heat stress when temperatures rise beyond their comfort range," said Dr Mohammed Bengoumi, a scientist with the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), who specialises in camel health and works in North Africa.
"In many parts of the Sahara, summer temperatures now frequently exceed 50C, increasing the risk of severe heat stress, particularly when accompanied by reduced vegetation cover, water scarcity, and limited access to shade," he told the BBC.
Professor Abdelmadjid Chehma at the University of Ghardaia in Algeria, who has conducted experimental works on camels in the Sahara Desert, has a similar conclusion.
"Our works show that prolonged day-and-night heat above 41 to 45C directly attack their cells," he told the BBC.
"Their immune system suffers because such heat levels damage their white blood cells and other cells because of stress, they [the cells] struggle to repair themselves and end up destroying themselves."
For camels this means when heat stress sets in, their metabolism slows down to limit internal heat production leading to sharp reduction in food intake resulting in lethargy and generalised fatigue.
That leads to drop in milk production and also causes reproductive disorders.
Professor Mohammed el Khasmi, animal hydrobiology expert at the University of Casablanca in Morocco, has a long list of effects of heat stress he and his team have observed on camels.
Weight loss, inflammation, muscle and bone related illnesses, chemical imbalance due to kidney malfunction, infectious diseases caused by parasites were a few among them, he said.
While extreme heat is the primary culprit, its impacts become severe when other factors like loss of vegetation and water, lack of shaded areas and inadequate veterinary services add up, experts say.
This is why many herders in Ethiopia have moved their camels from the northern region, where the animals were found historically, to the south where water and vegetation are relatively available, experts there say.
"And this is not the seasonal movement of the herders," said Daniel Gelan, professor and pastoralist development researcher with Vision University in Ethiopia.
"They are leaving the northern region for good because they can no longer sustain camel herding there because of extreme heat and drought," he told the BBC.
The Horn of Africa has been recovering from the longest and most severe recorded drought spanning from 2020 to 2023, but now it is seeing another round of the harsh condition, according to charity organisation Oxfam.
It said water prices in some parts of Somalia had risen by more than 2,000% because of the drought.
Umer, the cattle herder in Afar, said he was worried that an outbreak of disease could start killing his adult camels anytime now.
His concern is valid, according to Prof Chehma.
"While camels remain the livestock herders' last line of defence against the desert, the unprecedented intensity of current heatwaves directly threatens their vital functions, turning this historically resilient animal into a climate victim," he said.
Additional reporting by BBC Amharic's Firehiwot Kassa

title: Scottish Labour at a crossroads again as Sarwar jumps ship
summary: Anas Sarwar has never made a secret of his desire to hold high office, but where does it leave Scottish Labour?
full_text:
Scottish Labour at a crossroads again as Sarwar jumps ship
- Published
Anas Sarwar has never made a secret of his desire to hold high office.
It's only a matter of weeks since he offered himself to Scottish voters as a candidate to replace John Swinney as first minister.
That went spectacularly wrong. The SNP held power for a fifth consecutive term and Labour recorded their worst Holyrood result since devolution.
While the performance of the UK government under Sir Keir Starmer gets much of the blame, there is now a live debate in the party about Sarwar's strategy.
Questions are also being asked of Scottish Labour's campaign co-directors Jackie Baillie and Douglas Alexander.
Sarwar had said he would stick around as leader to steady the ship, but his swift exit contradicts that position and is a source of controversy for some.
There are those who see it as a reward for failure given the Holyrood defeat, even if Labour was able to beat the SNP in Scotland at the UK general election two years earlier.
There are those who see it as a reward for treachery given that Sarwar was the first senior Labour figure to call for Starmer to quit - a move that undermined the then prime minister, to the eventual benefit of Andy Burnham.
- Scottish Labour leader Anas Sarwar set to become a minister in Burnham's government - Published14 hours ago
 
- Who is Anas Sarwar? The Scottish Labour leader returning to UK politics - Published12 hours ago
 
- Who could be the new Scottish Labour leader? - Published10 hours ago
 
The prime minister's cabinet includes a number of those who took a stand against Starmer, so perhaps it should be no surprise that Burnham would want to make Sarwar a minister too.
There are also those who see Sarwar's appointment to the Lords in order to take up his government position as hypocritical.
Sarwar previously said he would not take a peerage, and both he and Andy Burnham have expressed support for replacing the Lords with a senate of the nations and regions.
By appointing another life peer within his first few days in office, is the new PM not sending out a completely contradictory signal?
I suppose he could argue that Sarwar is an ally on his agenda to rewire how British politics works and can now agitate for change from within.
As an experienced Labour leader in a devolved parliament with previous service as a Westminster MP, Sarwar might be particularly well placed to back up Burnham's case for devolving power from parliaments into cities and communities.
Their argument is that this could be a potential driver of economic growth.
Who could replace Sarwar?
Where does all this leave Scottish Labour? At yet another crossroads.
Sarwar was the party's tenth leader since the creation of the Scottish Parliament. They are now looking for number eleven.
The current deputy leader Jackie Baillie is in acting charge as she has been on a number of occasions in the past. She has always resisted running for the top job and will almost certainly do so again.
More likely candidates include MSP Michael Marra and Sarwar's probable replacement at Holyrood Monica Lennon - if the rules of the contest allow her to run.
The snag is that you have to be an MSP to stand for the leadership and she will not be able to take her seat until the Scottish Parliament returns in September.
My gut feeling - and it is only that - is that the party's ruling body, the Scottish Executive Committee, would want to accommodate her candidacy if she would like to run.
Other names that have been mentioned include MSPs Daniel Johnson and Paul Sweeney.
As I mentioned, there is already an internal debate about what went wrong in the 2026 Holyrood campaign and what the party needs to change. These conversations would fold in to any leadership contest.
The choice of personality is obviously important as is the party's future policy offer.
There's also likely to be discussion about whether or not Scottish Labour should split from the UK party.
Others might want to revisit their opposition to another independence referendum.
Huge questions for a party that used to dominate Scottish politics and hungers for a way back to power at Holyrood.
